body.translated_text: He who, having abandoned his primordial form, manifests for the benefit of the world in many ways,
whose heap of afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) is destroyed, who is like a serpent without venom, many-faced and of excellent enjoyment,
the source of all knowledge, girdled with serpents, whose delight is eternal—
that Lord of Serpents (<s>Ahīśa</s>), may he protect you—of white, pure body, the bestower of <s>yoga</s>, united in <s>yoga</s>.
Now, the teaching of <s>yoga</s>.
'Now' (<s>atha</s>)—this signifies the beginning of the subject.
The teaching of <s>yoga</s>—the scripture is commenced and should be understood.
<s>Yoga</s> is <s>samādhi</s> (absorption).
And that is a universal attribute of the mind (<s>citta</s>).
Restless (<s>kṣipta</s>), stupefied (<s>mūḍha</s>), distracted (<s>vikṣipta</s>), one-pointed (<s>ekāgra</s>), and arrested (<s>niruddha</s>)—these are the levels of the mind (<s>citta-bhūmi</s>).
When the mind is in the distracted state, the <s>samādhi</s> that is subordinate to distraction does not belong to the category of <s>yoga</s>.

But [the <s>samādhi</s>] that, when the mind is one-pointed, illuminates the true nature of the object, destroys the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), loosens the bonds of <s>karma</s>, and leads toward <s>nirodha</s> (cessation)—that is called <s>samprajñāta yoga</s> (cognitive <s>yoga</s>).

And that is accompanied by <s>vitarka</s> (deliberation), accompanied by <s>vicāra</s> (reflection), accompanied by <s>ānanda</s> (bliss), accompanied by <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness)—this we shall explain later.
But in the cessation of all mental modifications (<s>vṛttis</s>), [there is] <s>asamprajñāta samādhi</s> (non-cognitive absorption).
With the desire to characterize it, this <s>sūtra</s> was composed:
<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the modifications of the mind (<s>citta-vṛtti-nirodha</s>). [YS 1.2]
By the inclusion of the word 'all,' even <s>samprajñāta</s> is called <s>yoga</s>.
For the mind has the nature of the three <s>guṇas</s> (qualities), being characterized by luminosity (<s>prakhyā</s>), activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), and stability (<s>sthiti</s>).
The <s>sattva</s> (luminosity) aspect of the mind, mixed with <s>rajas</s> (activity) and <s>tamas</s> (inertia), becomes inclined toward sovereignty and attachment to sense-objects.
That very [<s>sattva</s>], pervaded by <s>tamas</s>, tends toward <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness), ignorance, non-dispassion, and powerlessness.

That very [<s>sattva</s>], with the veil of delusion removed, shining everywhere, pervaded by a mere trace of <s>rajas</s>, tends toward <s>dharma</s> (righteousness), knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.

That very [<s>sattva</s>], with even the trace of <s>rajas</s>-impurity removed, established in its own nature, consisting merely in the discrimination (<s>khyāti</s>) between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, tends toward <s>dharmamegha-dhyāna</s> (the rain-cloud of <s>dharma</s> meditation).
That the meditators (<s>dhyāyins</s>) call the supreme <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (higher meditation).

The power of awareness (<s>citiśakti</s>) is unchanging, non-transferable, pure, infinite, and of the nature of the <s>sattva-guṇa</s>; <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative knowledge) is the opposite of this—hence [it is distinct from <s>citiśakti</s>].
Therefore, in that [<s>vivekakhyāti</s>], when the mind has become dispassionate, it arrests even that discrimination.
In that state, [the mind] acquires <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions).
That is the seedless (<s>nirbīja</s>) <s>samādhi</s>.
Nothing is cognized therein—hence it is <s>asamprajñāta</s> (non-cognitive).
That <s>yoga</s>, the cessation of mental modifications, is twofold.
When the mind is in that state, due to the absence of objects, what is the nature of <s>Puruṣa</s>, who is of the nature of the awakening of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect)?
Then there is abiding in the Seer's (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) own nature. [YS 1.3]
Then the power of awareness (<s>citiśakti</s>) is established in its own nature, as in <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation/liberation).
But when the mind is in the emergent state (<s>vyutthāna</s>), although [the Seer] exists, it is not so.
How then? Because [the Seer's nature] has been shown to have objects of perception.
There is identification with the modifications elsewhere [i.e., in the non-yogic state]. [YS 1.4]
In the emergent state, the mental modifications—<s>Puruṣa</s> has a modification indistinguishable from those.
And thus [there is] the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Seeing is one and the same; discrimination (<s>khyāti</s>) alone is seeing.'
The mind, like a loadstone, beneficial merely by proximity, becomes an object of perception (<s>dṛśya</s>) for <s>Puruṣa</s>, its master (<s>svāmin</s>).
Therefore, <s>Puruṣa</s>'s awareness of mental modifications [constitutes] the beginningless (<s>anādi</s>) connection and its cause.
Those [modifications], moreover, are to be arrested, when the mind [contains] many [of them].
The modifications (<s>vṛttis</s>) are fivefold, afflicted (<s>kliṣṭa</s>) and unafflicted (<s>akliṣṭa</s>). [YS 1.5]
Those caused by afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>), forming the ground for the accumulation of the <s>karma</s>-repository (<s>karmāśaya</s>), are afflicted.
Those having discrimination (<s>khyāti</s>) as their object, opposing the dominion of the <s>guṇas</s>, are unafflicted.
Even those fallen in the stream of affliction are [sometimes] unafflicted.
Even in the gaps between afflictions, they are unafflicted.
In the gaps of the unafflicted, [the modifications become] afflicted.
<s>Saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) of the same kind are produced by the modifications alone.
And by the <s>saṃskāras</s>, the modifications [are produced].
Thus the wheel of modifications and <s>saṃskāras</s> revolves ceaselessly.
That mind, being thus constituted, when its purpose is fulfilled, either abides in a form resembling the Self or goes to dissolution (<s>pralaya</s>).
Those modifications, both afflicted and unafflicted, are fivefold.
Valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>), error (<s>viparyaya</s>), conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>), sleep (<s>nidrā</s>), and memory (<s>smṛti</s>). [YS 1.6]
Perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), inference (<s>anumāna</s>), and verbal testimony (<s>āgama</s>) are the valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). [YS 1.7]

The modification of the mind that, through the channel of the senses, due to the mind's coloring by external objects, having those objects as its content, is primarily directed toward the ascertainment of the particular [aspect] of the object that possesses both general and particular characteristics—this is perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) as a valid means of knowledge.
The result is <s>Puruṣa</s>'s awareness of the mental modification, which is undifferentiated [from the object].
We shall establish later that <s>Puruṣa</s> is the experiencer (<s>pratisaṃvedī</s>).

The relation that exists in things of the same class as the thing to be inferred, persisting [in them], and excluded from things of different classes—the modification primarily directed toward the ascertainment of the general [aspect], having that as its object, is inference (<s>anumāna</s>).

Just as the moon and stars, by virtue of reaching different places, possess movement—like <s>Caitra</s> [who is seen moving]; but <s>Vindhya</s>, by virtue of not reaching [different places], does not possess movement.

An object seen or inferred by a reliable person (<s>āpta</s>) is taught to another through words for the purpose of transmitting one's own knowledge; the modification in the listener arising from words, having that meaning as its object, is verbal testimony (<s>āgama</s>).
That verbal testimony whose speaker is not trustworthy regarding the meaning, and who has not [directly] seen or inferred the meaning—that testimony is unstable.
But when the original speaker has [directly] seen or inferred the meaning, it would be unshakable.
Error (<s>viparyaya</s>) is false knowledge, not established in the nature of that [object]. [YS 1.8]
Why is that not a valid means of knowledge?
Because it is contradicted by valid knowledge.
Since valid knowledge has an actually existing object as its content.
There, the contradiction of what is not valid knowledge by valid knowledge is observed.
For example, the perception of two moons is contradicted by the [valid] perception of one moon.

This [error] has five stages and is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance); <s>avidyā</s>, <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness), <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life) are the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions).
These very [five], by their own names, are <s>tamas</s> (darkness), <s>moha</s> (delusion), <s>mahāmoha</s> (great delusion), <s>tāmisra</s> (gloom), and <s>andhatāmisra</s> (blind darkness).
These will be discussed in connection with the impurities of the mind.
Conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>) is [a modification] following upon verbal knowledge, devoid of [corresponding] reality. [YS 1.9]
It does not ascend to [the level of] valid knowledge.
Nor does it ascend to error.
Even though devoid of reality, a usage based on the power of verbal knowledge is observed.
For example: 'Consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) is the essential nature of <s>Puruṣa</s>.'
When consciousness itself is <s>Puruṣa</s>, then what is predicated here of what?
And there is a [mental] modification in predication.
Just as [one says] '<s>Caitra</s>'s cow.'
Likewise, <s>Puruṣa</s>, whose objective properties are denied, is actionless—[as in] 'the arrow stands,' 'it will stand,' 'it stood.'
In the cessation of movement, only the bare meaning of the verbal root is understood.
Similarly, '<s>Puruṣa</s> is of the nature of non-origination'—only the absence of the property of origination is understood, not a positive property belonging to <s>Puruṣa</s>.
Therefore that property is conceptually constructed, and yet there is practical usage by means of it.
Sleep (<s>nidrā</s>) is the modification supported by the cognition of absence. [YS 1.10]
And that, upon awakening, is recognized as a specific cognition from [subsequent] reflection.
How so? 'I slept happily;'
'my mind is clear; it makes my understanding sharp.'
'I slept badly; my mind is dull; it wanders, unstable.'
'I slept heavily; I am confused;'
'my limbs are heavy;'
'my mind is fatigued;'
'it stands as if idle and stolen.'
Indeed, this recognition upon awakening would not occur in the absence of the experience of a [specific] cognition, nor would memories dependent on and pertaining to that [cognition] exist.
Therefore, sleep is a specific cognition.
And in <s>samādhi</s>, it must be arrested like other cognitions.
Memory (<s>smṛti</s>) is the non-deprivation of an experienced object. [YS 1.11]
Does the mind remember the cognition or the object?

The cognition, colored by the apprehended [object], manifesting the appearance of both the apprehended (<s>grāhya</s>) and the apprehender (<s>grahaṇa</s>), initiates a <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) of the same kind.
That <s>saṃskāra</s>, revealing its own expression, generates memory of that very form, possessing the dual nature of both the apprehended and the apprehender.
Therein, intellectual cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) is preceded by the form of apprehension.
Memory is preceded by the form of the apprehended.
And that [memory] is twofold: [that whose] object of recall has been [previously] cultivated, and [that whose] object of recall has not been cultivated.
In dream, [the object of recall has been] cultivated.
But in the waking state, [the object of recall has] not been cultivated.
All memories arise from the experience of valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory.
And all these modifications are characterized by pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>).
And pleasure, pain, and delusion will be explained [in connection with] the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions).
Attachment (<s>rāga</s>) is the residual impression of pleasure.
Aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) is the residual impression of pain.
And delusion (<s>moha</s>) is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>).
All these modifications are to be arrested.
In their arrest, there arises either <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s> (cognitive absorption) or <s>asamprajñāta</s> (non-cognitive absorption).
Now, what is the means for their arrest?
Their arrest [is achieved] through practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) and dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>). [YS 1.12]
The river of the mind (<s>cittanadī</s>) flows in both directions—it flows toward the good and it flows toward evil.
That which inclines toward <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) and slopes toward the object of discrimination (<s>viveka</s>)—that carries the good.
That which inclines toward <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) and slopes toward the object of non-discrimination—that carries evil.
Therein, by dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>), the stream toward [sense-]objects is blocked.
By the practice of the vision of discrimination, the stream of discrimination is opened—thus the cessation of mental modifications depends on both.
Therein, effort toward steadiness is practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>). [YS 1.13]
Steadiness (<s>sthiti</s>) is the tranquil flow of the mind devoid of modifications.
The effort for that [purpose] is vigor, enthusiasm.
The desire to accomplish that, the performance of the means for that—is practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>).
[Sūtra I.14:] But that [practice] becomes firmly grounded when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion.
[Bhāṣya:] Cultivated for a long time, cultivated without interruption, cultivated with devotion.
When accomplished through austerity (<s>tapas</s>), celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), and faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), it possesses devotion and becomes firmly grounded.
It is not quickly overwhelmed by the impressions of emergence (<s>vyutthāna-saṃskāra</s>) — that is the meaning.
[Sūtra I.15:] <s>Vairāgya</s> (dispassion) is the consciousness of mastery (<s>vaśīkāra-saṃjñā</s>) in one who is free from craving for objects seen or heard about.

[Bhāṣya:] For one who is free from craving for visible objects such as women, food and drink, and sovereignty, and who is free from craving for objects heard about in scripture such as the attainment of heaven, of the bodiless state (<s>videha</s>), and of absorption in <s>Prakṛti</s> (<s>prakṛtilaya</s>) — for one whose mind, even when in contact with divine or non-divine objects, sees the defects of sense-objects — through the strength of discriminative discernment (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), the consciousness of mastery (<s>vaśīkāra-saṃjñā</s>), which is of the nature of non-engagement, devoid of what is to be rejected or accepted, is <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion).
[Sūtra I.16:] That is the supreme [dispassion] — the absence of craving for the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents of nature), due to the realization of <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self).

[Bhāṣya:] One who is dispassionate toward objects seen and heard about, having seen their defects, and who, through the practice of the vision of <s>Puruṣa</s>, has an intellect nourished by the purity and discrimination of that [<s>Puruṣa</s>], becomes dispassionate toward the <s>guṇas</s> with their manifest and unmanifest properties.
That twofold is <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion).
Of these, the latter is nothing but the clarity of knowledge.

When that arises, the <s>yogin</s> of awakened discernment thinks thus: 'What was to be attained has been attained; the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) that were to be diminished have been diminished; the chain of existence with its closely linked segments has been severed—that chain by whose unbroken continuity one is born after dying and dies after being born.'
The ultimate limit of knowledge is <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion).
For nothing other than <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute liberation) is its immediate consequence.

[Question:] Now, how is the <s>samādhi</s> called '<s>samprajñāta</s>' (cognitive) described, when the mental modifications have been suppressed through the twofold means [of practice and dispassion]?
[Sūtra I.17:] <s>Samprajñāta</s> [samādhi] is accompanied by <s>vitarka</s> (deliberation), <s>vicāra</s> (reflection), <s>ānanda</s> (bliss), and <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness).
[Bhāṣya:] <s>Vitarka</s> (deliberation) is the gross engagement of the mind with its object.
<s>Vicāra</s> (reflection) is the subtle [engagement].
<s>Ānanda</s> (bliss) is joy.
<s>Asmitā</s> (I-am-ness) is the unitary awareness of self-identity.
Of these, the first <s>samādhi</s>, accompanied by all four [factors], is <s>savitarka</s> (with deliberation).
The second, devoid of <s>vitarka</s>, is <s>savicāra</s> (with reflection).
The third, devoid of <s>vicāra</s>, is <s>sānanda</s> (with bliss).
The fourth, devoid of that [bliss], consists of <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness) alone.
All these <s>samādhis</s> have a support (<s>ālambana</s>).
[Question:] Now, what is the means and what is the nature of <s>asamprajñāta samādhi</s> (non-cognitive absorption)?
[Sūtra I.18:] The other [<s>samādhi</s>], preceded by the practice of the cause of cessation (<s>virāma-pratyaya</s>), has only <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) remaining.
[Bhāṣya:] The cessation of all mental modifications, with only <s>saṃskāras</s> remaining, is the <s>nirodha</s> (suppression) of the mind — the <s>asamprajñāta samādhi</s>.
Its means is the supreme <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion).
For practice with a support does not serve as the means for that; therefore the cessation-cognition (<s>virāma-pratyaya</s>), which is objectless, is made into a support.
And that is devoid of content.

For the mind, preceded by the practice of that [objectless cognition], becomes as if it has arrived at non-existence, without support — this is the seedless (<s>nirbīja</s>) <s>samādhi</s>, the <s>asamprajñāta</s>.
That [<s>asamprajñāta samādhi</s>] is indeed of two kinds: caused by means (<s>upāya-pratyaya</s>) and caused by existence (<s>bhava-pratyaya</s>).
[Sūtra I.19:] That caused by means belongs to the <s>yogins</s>.
[Sūtra I.19:] That caused by existence belongs to the <s>videhas</s> (bodiless beings) and those absorbed in <s>Prakṛti</s> (<s>prakṛtilayas</s>).
[Bhāṣya:] Of the <s>videhas</s>, [among] the gods, it is caused by existence.

For they, experiencing through the mind a state resembling <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) by means of their own <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) alone, pass through the ripening of their own impressions in corresponding births.

Likewise, those absorbed in <s>Prakṛti</s>, when the mind has dissolved into <s>Prakṛti</s> while its function still remains, experience a state resembling <s>kaivalya</s> — until the mind returns again by the force of that function.
[Sūtra I.20:] For others, [<s>asamprajñāta samādhi</s>] is preceded by faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), vigor (<s>vīrya</s>), memory (<s>smṛti</s>), <s>samādhi</s>, and wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>).
[Bhāṣya:] That caused by means belongs to the <s>yogins</s>.
Faith (<s>śraddhā</s>) is the serenity of the mind.
For she, like a benevolent mother, protects the <s>yogin</s>.
For one who has faith and seeks discrimination, vigor (<s>vīrya</s>) arises.
For one in whom vigor has arisen, memory (<s>smṛti</s>) presents itself.
And when memory has presented itself, the mind, free from agitation, becomes absorbed in <s>samādhi</s>.
For one whose mind is absorbed, the discriminative wisdom (<s>prajñā-viveka</s>) unfolds.
By which one knows the object as it truly is.
Through the practice of that [sequence] and through dispassion toward the respective objects, <s>asamprajñāta samādhi</s> arises.
[Bhāṣya:] Now, these nine [types of] <s>yogins</s> have means that are mild, moderate, or intense.
Namely: one of mild means, one of moderate means, and one of intense means.
Among these, one of mild means is threefold: of mild intensity, of moderate intensity, and of keen intensity.
Likewise, one of moderate means, and likewise one of intense means.
Among those of intense means—
[Sūtra I.21:] For those of keen intensity, [<s>samādhi</s>] is near.
The attainment of <s>samādhi</s> and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> come [quickly].
[Sūtra I.22:] Even among these, there is a further distinction due to [the practice being] mild, moderate, or intense.
Mildly keen, moderately keen, and intensely keen.
Even from that there is a further distinction.

From that distinction also, for one of mildly keen intensity [<s>samādhi</s>] is near; for one of moderately keen intensity, nearer; for one of intensely keen intensity with intense means, the nearest is the attainment and fruit of <s>samādhi</s>.
[Question:] Does <s>samādhi</s> come nearest only from this?
Or is there some other means for its attainment or not?
[Sūtra I.23:] Or, through devotion to <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord).
[Bhāṣya:] Through <s>praṇidhāna</s> (devotion), a special form of devotion (<s>bhakti</s>), <s>Īśvara</s>, being favorably inclined, bestows grace upon that [<s>yogin</s>] through mere contemplation.
Through that mere contemplation of him, the <s>yogin</s> attains the nearest attainment of <s>samādhi</s> and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s>.
[Question:] Now, who is this <s>Īśvara</s>, distinct from <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self)?
[Sūtra I.24:] <s>Īśvara</s> is a special <s>Puruṣa</s>, untouched by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s> (actions), <s>vipāka</s> (their results), and <s>āśayas</s> (latent deposits).
[Bhāṣya:] The <s>kleśas</s> are <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and the rest.
<s>Karmas</s> are wholesome and unwholesome actions.
<s>Vipāka</s> (ripening) is their result.
<s>Āśayas</s> (latent deposits) are the tendencies (<s>vāsanās</s>) corresponding to those.
And these, though existing in the mind, are attributed to <s>Puruṣa</s>, for he is the experiencer of their fruit.
Just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the lord.
He who is untouched by this experience — that special <s>Puruṣa</s> is <s>Īśvara</s>.
[Objection:] There are indeed many who have attained <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) — they too are liberated beings (<s>kevalins</s>).
For they, having cut the three bonds, have attained <s>kaivalya</s>; but <s>Īśvara</s>'s connection with those [bonds] was neither past nor future.
Just as for a liberated being the prior limit of bondage is recognized — not so for <s>Īśvara</s>.
Or just as for one absorbed in <s>Prakṛti</s>, a later limit of bondage is conceivable — not so for <s>Īśvara</s>.
He is indeed always free, always the Lord.
[Question:] Now, this eternal supremacy of <s>Īśvara</s>, arising from his taking on a supremely pure <s>sattva</s> — is it caused or uncaused?
Scripture (<s>śāstra</s>) is its cause.
And what is the cause of scripture? Supremely pure <s>sattva</s> is its cause.
The relationship between these two — scripture and supremacy — which exist in the <s>sattva</s> of <s>Īśvara</s>, is beginningless.
From this it follows that <s>Īśvara</s> is always the Lord, always free.
And that lordship of his is free from equality or superiority [by any other].
It is not surpassed by any other lordship.
Whatever would surpass it, that itself would be it [i.e., would itself be <s>Īśvara</s>].
Therefore, that in which lordship reaches its ultimate limit — that is <s>Īśvara</s>.
Nor is there any lordship equal to it.

Because if two beings of equal power simultaneously desired contradictory things — 'Let this be new,' 'Let this be old' — the success of one would entail the frustration of the other's sovereign will, [proving] its inferiority.
And for two of equal power, the simultaneous attainment of desired objects is impossible,
due to the contradictory nature of the objects.
Therefore, he whose lordship is free from equality and superiority — he alone is <s>Īśvara</s>.
And he is the special <s>Puruṣa</s>.
Moreover:
[Sūtra I.25:] In him, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed.

[Bhāṣya:] That which is the grasping of the past, future, and present — whether individually or collectively — and of what is beyond the senses, as 'little' or 'much,' is the seed of omniscience. Where this, increasing, reaches its unsurpassed [limit] — he is the Omniscient One.
There is an ultimate limit for the seed of omniscience, since it is subject to degrees — like a measurable quantity.
Where knowledge reaches its ultimate limit, he is the Omniscient One.
And he is the special <s>Puruṣa</s>.
And inference, which terminates only in a general conclusion, is not capable of determining the specific characteristics.
The specific knowledge of his name and other particulars must be sought from scripture (<s>āgama</s>).
Even when there is no benefit to himself, the benefit of living beings is his purpose.
'Through the teaching of the doctrine of knowledge, I shall deliver beings caught in <s>saṃsāra</s> at the time of creation, dissolution, and great dissolution.'

And thus it is said: 'The primal knower, the blessed supreme sage, having assumed a created mind (<s>nirmāṇa-citta</s>), out of compassion taught the <s>tantra</s> (systematic doctrine) to <s>Āsuri</s> who desired to know.'
He is this [<s>Īśvara</s>] —
[Sūtra I.26:] He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time.
[Bhāṣya:] For the teachers of the ancients are limited by time.
He with respect to whom time does not serve as a limiting factor — he is the teacher even of the ancients.
Just as at the beginning of this creation he is established as having been active, so too he should be understood at the beginning of past creations also.
[Sūtra I.27:] His designator is <s>Praṇava</s> (<s>Oṃ</s>).
[Bhāṣya:] <s>Īśvara</s> is the thing designated (<s>vācya</s>) by <s>Praṇava</s>.
[Question:] Is the relationship of designator and designated between them conventional, or is it established like the relationship between a lamp and its light?
The relationship of this designated thing with its designator is established [eternally].
Convention merely indicates the already established meaning of <s>Īśvara</s>.
Just as the relationship between father and son is established [by nature] and is made manifest through convention — 'This is his father, this is his son' —
even in other creations, convention is made in the same way, depending on the power of designator and designated.
The followers of <s>Āgama</s> (scriptural tradition) maintain: 'The relationship between word and meaning is eternal, due to the eternity of the convention.'
[Sūtra I.28:] For the <s>yogin</s> who has understood the relationship of designator and designated —
[Sūtra I.28:] Its repetition (<s>japa</s>) and contemplation of its meaning.
[Bhāṣya:] The repetition of <s>Praṇava</s> and the contemplation of <s>Īśvara</s>, who is designated by <s>Praṇava</s>.
Thus, for this yogin who recites <s>praṇava</s> (Oṃ) and contemplates its meaning, the mind becomes one-pointed.
And thus it has been said: 'From self-study one should practice yoga; from yoga one should practice self-study. Through the perfection of self-study and yoga, the supreme Self is illuminated.'
Moreover, this [also] comes about for him:
[Sūtra:] From that [practice], the attainment of inward-directed consciousness and also the absence of obstacles.
The obstacles, beginning with disease, do not arise through devotion to <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord).
The vision of one's own true nature also arises for him.

Just as <s>Īśvara</s> is a <s>Puruṣa</s> (consciousness) that is pure, serene, absolute, and unaffected [by afflictions], so too this [yogin] attains that <s>Puruṣa</s> who perceives through the intellect.
Now, what are the obstacles that are the distractions of the mind?
What are they, and how many are there?

[Sūtra:] Disease, dullness, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, non-abstention, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability — these are the distractions of the mind; they are the obstacles.
There are nine obstacles that are distractions of the mind.
These occur together with the mental modifications (<s>cittavṛtti</s>).
In the absence of these, the previously mentioned mental modifications do not arise.
Disease (<s>vyādhi</s>) is an imbalance of the bodily constituents (<s>dhātus</s>), vital essences (<s>rasas</s>), and sense-organs (<s>karaṇas</s>).
Dullness (<s>styāna</s>) is the incapacity for action of the mind.
Doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>) is a cognition that touches both alternatives — 'it may be thus, or it may not be thus.'
Heedlessness (<s>pramāda</s>) is the non-cultivation of the means to <s>samādhi</s>.
Laziness (<s>ālasya</s>) is non-activity due to the heaviness of body and mind.
Non-abstention (<s>avirati</s>) is the craving whose nature is the contact of the mind with sense-objects.
Erroneous perception (<s>bhrāntidarśana</s>) is false knowledge (<s>viparyayajñāna</s>).
Failure to attain a stage (<s>alabdhabhūmikatva</s>) is the non-attainment of a stage of <s>samādhi</s>.
Instability (<s>anavasthitatva</s>) is the mind's failure to remain established when a stage has been attained.
For when <s>samādhi</s> is attained, the mind should become established in that state.
These nine mental distractions are called the impurities of yoga, the adversaries of yoga, the obstacles to yoga.
[Sūtra:] Suffering, mental distress, trembling of the body, and [disturbed] inhalation and exhalation accompany the distractions.
Suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>) is of three kinds: pertaining to the self (<s>ādhyātmika</s>), pertaining to beings (<s>ādhibhautika</s>), and pertaining to the divine [forces] (<s>ādhidaivika</s>).
That by which living beings are afflicted, and for whose removal they strive — that is suffering.
Mental distress (<s>daurmanasya</s>) is the agitation of the mind due to the obstruction of desire.
That which causes the limbs to shake and tremble — that is trembling of the body (<s>aṅgamejayatva</s>).
When <s>prāṇa</s> (the life-breath) draws in the external air, that is inhalation (<s>śvāsa</s>).
When it expels the air from the body cavity, that is exhalation (<s>praśvāsa</s>).
These accompany the distractions — they arise in one whose mind is distracted.
They do not arise in one whose mind is concentrated.
Now, these distractions, which are adversaries of <s>samādhi</s>, are to be restrained by those same two [means] — <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) and <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion).
Therein, summarizing the object of practice, [the author] states this:
[Sūtra:] For the prevention of those [obstacles], the practice of [concentration on] a single principle.
For the prevention of distractions, one should practice [fixing] the mind upon a single principle as its support.
For one whose mind is momentary and whose cognition is determined by each [successive] object, all the mind is one-pointed [by their definition] — there is simply no distracted [state].
But if this [mind] is withdrawn from all [objects] and concentrated upon a single object, then it becomes one-pointed — therefore it is not [merely] determined by each object.

And for one who considers the mind to be one-pointed [merely because it consists of] a flow of similar cognitions — if one-pointedness is a property of the flowing mind, then there is no single [mind], since the flowing mind is momentary.

If, however, it is a property of the cognition that is a component of the flow, then every [such cognition], whether flowing with similar or dissimilar cognitions, is one-pointed by virtue of being determined by its [respective] object — and thus the impossibility of a distracted mind [follows, which is absurd].
Therefore, the mind is one, has many objects, and is enduring.
And if cognitions — which are different in nature and unconnected — were to arise from multiple [momentary] minds, then how could one [mind] be the rememberer of what was seen by another cognition?
And how could one cognition be the experiencer of the karmic residue accumulated by another cognition?
Even if somehow managed, this invites the objection of the 'cow-dung-milk-pudding' fallacy.
Moreover, the denial of one's own experience would follow if the mind were [accepted as] different [at each moment].
How so? 'What I saw, I touch; and what I touched, I see' — thus the 'I'-cognition, when there is difference among all cognitions, presents itself as non-different in the cognizer.
This 'I'-cognition, whose object is a single cognizer and whose nature is non-difference — how could it, occurring in absolutely different minds, refer to one common cognizer?
And this 'I'-cognition, whose nature is non-difference, is grasped by one's own experience.
And the authority of direct perception is not overridden by any other means of valid knowledge.
Moreover, other means of valid knowledge acquire their validity only through the power of direct perception.
Therefore, the mind is one, has many objects, and is enduring.
For this enduring mind, the purification is prescribed by this <s>śāstra</s> (teaching). How [is this done]?

[Sūtra:] Through the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward [those who are in states of] happiness, suffering, virtue, and vice [respectively], there comes the serenity of the mind.
Therein, toward all living beings who have attained enjoyment of happiness, one should cultivate friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>);
toward those who are suffering, compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>);
toward those of virtuous nature, joy (<s>muditā</s>);
toward those of sinful disposition, equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>).
For one cultivating thus, a wholesome mental disposition arises.
And thereby the mind becomes serene.
Being serene, it becomes one-pointed and attains a state of stability.
[Sūtra:] Or [stability of mind is attained] by expulsion and retention of breath.

The expulsion (<s>pracchardana</s>) is a special effort of exhaling the air from the body cavity through the nostrils; retention (<s>vidhāraṇa</s>) is <s>prāṇāyāma</s> — by these two, one should bring about the stability of the mind.
[Sūtra:] Or a sensory activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>) that has arisen, which binds the mind to stability.
When one concentrates on the tip of the nose, the divine perception of fragrance that arises — that is the olfactory activity.
At the tip of the tongue — the perception of taste.
At the palate — the perception of form.
At the middle of the tongue — the perception of touch.
At the root of the tongue — the perception of sound. These activities, having arisen, bind the mind to stability, dispel doubt, and become the gateway to the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>.

By this, the sensory activity that arises regarding the moon, sun, planets, gems, lamp-light, and the like should also be understood as pertaining to objects. For although the true nature of things is understood through the respective scriptures, inference, and the teacher's instruction, and is indeed real,

due to their capacity to establish things as they truly are — nevertheless, as long as even some small part is not directly perceived by one's own faculties, everything remains as if remote; it does not produce firm conviction regarding subtle matters such as <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) and the like.
Therefore, to reinforce what is taught by scripture, inference, and the teacher's instruction, some particular object must necessarily be made directly perceptible.
Therein, when even one part of the objects taught [by these sources] is directly perceived, all subtle objects including liberation are believed [with conviction].
It is for this very purpose that this purification of the mind is prescribed.

When, among the unrestrained activities, the mastery-cognition (<s>vaśīkārasaṃjñā</s>) pertaining to that object has arisen, [the mind] would be capable of directly perceiving each of those [subtle] objects.
And when this is the case, faith, energy, memory, and <s>samādhi</s> will proceed for him without obstruction.
[Sūtra:] Or [that activity which is] sorrowless and luminous.
'A sensory activity that has arisen, which binds the mind to stability' — this [qualification] carries over [from the previous sūtra].

When one concentrates on the lotus of the heart, the awareness of the intellect [arises] — for the <s>sattva</s> (essence) of the intellect is luminous and space-like. Through the mastery of stability therein, the activity manifests in the forms of the radiance of the sun, moon, planets, and gems.
Likewise, the mind that has attained [the state of pure] 'I-am-ness' (<s>asmitā</s>) becomes like a vast, waveless ocean — peaceful, infinite, consisting of mere I-am-ness.
Where this has been said: 'Having found that infinitesimal Self, one cognizes thus: "I am"' — to that extent [is the realization].
This twofold [activity] — pertaining to objects [and] sorrowless, and consisting of mere I-am-ness — is called 'luminous' (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>).
By which the yogin's mind attains a state of stability.
[Sūtra:] Or the mind [is stabilized by taking as its object] one who is free from passion.
The yogin's mind, colored by [contemplating] the mind of one who is free from passion, attains a state of stability.
[Sūtra:] Or [by having as its] support the knowledge [arising from] dream or sleep.
Or having the knowledge [arising from] dream as its support, or having the knowledge [arising from] sleep as its support — taking that form, the yogin's mind attains a state of stability.
[Sūtra:] Or by meditation on whatever is agreeable.
Whatever is agreeable [to the yogin], that alone one should meditate upon.
Therein, having gained stability [in one object], the mind attains stability elsewhere as well.
[Sūtra:] His mastery extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude.
When settling into the subtle, the mind attains a state of stability extending to the atomic level.
When settling into the gross, the mind attains a state of stability extending to the greatest magnitude.
Thus, for one who pursues both extremes, the unimpeded [mastery] that results is the supreme mastery (<s>vaśīkāra</s>).
Through that mastery, the yogin's mind becomes complete and no longer requires the purification effected by practice.
Now, for the mind that has attained stability — what is the nature and what is the object of <s>samāpatti</s> (cognitive absorption)? To that it is said:

[Sūtra:] <s>Samāpatti</s> (cognitive absorption) is, for one whose mental modifications have diminished, like a pure crystal — the taking on of the color of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, [with the mind] resting upon and assuming the form of that [object].
'For one whose mental modifications have diminished' means one whose cognitions have subsided.
'Like a pure crystal' — this is the introduction of an analogy.

Just as a crystal, due to differences in what is placed near it, appears colored by each form and manifests with the appearance of the form of [its] support — so the mind, colored by the object to be grasped (<s>grāhya</s>), having attained absorption in the graspable, manifests with the form and appearance of the graspable.
When colored by the subtle elements (<s>bhūtasūkṣma</s>), it attains absorption in the subtle elements and becomes an appearance of the form of the subtle elements.
Likewise, when colored by a gross object, it attains absorption in the gross form and becomes an appearance of the gross form.
Similarly, when colored by the distinctions of all objects, it assumes the form of all distinctions and appears as having the form of everything.
Similarly, this should be understood with respect to the instruments of cognition (<s>grahaṇa</s>), i.e., the sense organs (<s>indriyas</s>) as well.
When colored by the object that is the instrument of cognition, it assumes the form of the instrument of cognition and shines forth in the form of that instrument of cognition.
Similarly, when colored by the object that is the cognizer, <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self), it assumes the form of the cognizer-<s>Puruṣa</s> and shines forth in the form of the cognizer-<s>Puruṣa</s>.
Similarly, when colored by the object that is the liberated <s>Puruṣa</s>, it assumes the form of the liberated <s>Puruṣa</s> and shines forth in the form of the liberated <s>Puruṣa</s>.

Thus, for the mind that has become like a transparent jewel, in regard to the cognizer, the instrument of cognition, and the object of cognition—i.e., <s>Puruṣa</s>, the senses, and the elements—the state of being colored by what is placed near it, the assumption of the form of that object when resting upon them, that is called <s>samāpatti</s> (cognitive absorption).
Therein, <s>savitarkā samāpatti</s> (absorption with deliberation) is that which is mixed with the distinctions of word, meaning, and knowledge.
For instance, the word 'cow,' the object 'cow,' and the cognition 'cow'—though these are distinct, they are apprehended as undifferentiated.
But when analyzed, the properties of the word are different, the properties of the object are different, and the properties of the cognition are different—their paths are distinct.

When the <s>yogī</s> in absorption takes up an object such as a cow in the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>, if it arises pervaded by the distinctions of word, meaning, and knowledge, that mixed absorption is called <s>savitarkā</s> (with deliberation).

But when, through the purification of memory from verbal conventions, the object stands in the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s> that is devoid of the distinctions of knowledge from scripture and inference, established in its own essential nature alone, and is apprehended solely in its own essential form—
that is <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s> (absorption without deliberation).
That is the supreme direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>).
And that is the seed of scriptural knowledge (<s>śruti</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>).
From that, scriptural knowledge and inference arise.
But that vision of <s>samādhi</s> does not coexist with knowledge from scripture and inference.
Therefore, the <s>yogī</s>'s vision born of <s>nirvitarka samādhi</s> is unmixed with any other means of valid knowledge.
The characteristic of this <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s> is now indicated by the <s>sūtra</s>:
[Yogasūtra I.43:] When memory is purified, the mind, as if empty of its own form, shining forth with the object alone—that is <s>nirvitarkā</s> (without deliberation).

When the wisdom, purified through the cleansing of memory from the distinctions of verbal convention, scripture, and inferential knowledge, is colored by the nature of the object to be cognized, and as if abandoning its own nature as wisdom—which is of the nature of cognition—becomes as if having assumed the very nature of the object alone, that is then <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s>.

And thus it has been explained: the worldly object, such as a cow or a pot, which is of the nature of an object constituted by a particular aggregation of atoms, is approached through a single cognition.
And that particular configuration, being a common property of the subtle elements, being intrinsic to them, inferred from its manifest effect, manifests when colored by its own manifestors.
And upon the arising of another property, as in a potsherd, it disappears.
This property is called <s>avayavin</s> (the composite whole).
That which is one, great, minute, tangible, characterized by action, and impermanent—it is through such a composite entity that worldly transactions are carried out.
For one who holds it to be unreal, that particular aggregation is merely nominal.

And the subtle cause being imperceptible, and for one who rejects conceptual distinctions, since there is no composite entity, all knowledge would be established in what is not its true form—thus nearly all knowledge would turn out to be false.
And then, what would right knowledge be, in the absence of an object?
Whatever is perceived is taught as being a composite entity.
Therefore, the composite entity exists—that which has entered into worldly transactions involving greatness and the like—and it becomes the object of <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s>.
By this very explanation, <s>savicārā</s> (with reflection) and <s>nirvicārā</s> (without reflection) absorptions, which have subtle objects, are also explained.

Therein, the absorption that occurs in regard to the subtle elements, which have manifest properties and are delimited by space, time, cause, and experience—that is called <s>savicārā</s> (with reflection).
There too, that which is graspable by a single cognition, characterized by manifest properties, having become the support as a subtle element, presents itself in the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>.

But the absorption that occurs in regard to subtle elements which are undifferentiated by quiescent, arisen, and indeterminate properties in every way and from every direction, which follow all properties and are of the nature of all properties—that is called <s>nirvicārā</s> (without reflection).
For the subtle element of such a nature, having become the support in this very form, colors the nature of the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>.
And when wisdom becomes as if empty of its own form, consisting of the object alone, then it is called <s>nirvicārā</s>.
Therein, <s>savitarkā</s> and <s>nirvitarkā</s> have gross objects, while <s>savicārā</s> and <s>nirvicārā</s> have subtle objects.
Thus, for both gross and subtle objects, the abandonment of conceptual distinction through <s>nirvitarkā</s> alone has been explained.
And the subtlety of the object extends up to <s>aliṅga</s> (the unmanifest <s>Prakṛti</s>).
For the earth atom, the <s>gandha-tanmātra</s> (subtle element of smell) is the subtle object.
For the water atom, the <s>rasa-tanmātra</s> (subtle element of taste).
For the fire atom, the <s>rūpa-tanmātra</s> (subtle element of form).
For the wind atom, the <s>sparśa-tanmātra</s> (subtle element of touch).
For space, the <s>śabda-tanmātra</s> (subtle element of sound).
For these tanmātras, <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (the ego-principle) is the subtle object.
And for <s>ahaṃkāra</s> too, <s>liṅgamātra</s> (the Great Principle, <s>Mahat</s>) is the subtle object.
And for <s>liṅgamātra</s> too, <s>aliṅga</s> (the unmanifest <s>Prakṛti</s>) is the subtle object.
And there is nothing subtler than <s>aliṅga</s>.
[Objection:] 'But <s>Puruṣa</s> is subtle.' True.
The subtlety of <s>aliṅga</s> relative to <s>liṅga</s> is of the same order, but not so for <s>Puruṣa</s>.
Rather, <s>Puruṣa</s> is not the material cause of <s>liṅga</s>, but is its efficient cause.
Therefore, the subtlety of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) has been explained as unsurpassed.
These alone constitute <s>sabīja samādhi</s> (concentration with seed).
These four <s>samāpattis</s> have external objects as their seed; hence the <s>samādhi</s> too is 'with seed.'
Therein, with a gross object: <s>savitarka</s> and <s>nirvitarka</s>; with a subtle object: <s>savicāra</s> and <s>nirvicāra</s>—thus <s>samādhi</s> is enumerated as fourfold.
[Yogasūtra I.47:] Upon the clarity of <s>nirvicāra</s> samādhi, there arises inner luminosity (<s>adhyātmaprasāda</s>).

When the <s>buddhi-sattva</s> (the luminous essence of the intellect), whose nature is illumination, is freed from the covering impurity of defilement and is not overpowered by <s>rajas</s> (activity) and <s>tamas</s> (inertia), its clear, steady flow is called <s>vaiśāradya</s> (mastery).
When this mastery of <s>nirvicāra samādhi</s> arises, then the <s>yogī</s> attains inner luminosity—a clear light of wisdom whose object is reality itself, not following any sequence.

And thus it has been said: 'Having ascended to the clarity of wisdom, free from sorrow, the wise one looks down upon the sorrowing people, as one standing on a mountain looks down upon those standing on the ground.'
[Yogasūtra I.48:] The wisdom therein is <s>ṛtambharā</s> (truth-bearing).
The wisdom that arises in one whose mind is concentrated therein bears the name <s>ṛtambharā</s> (truth-bearing).
And it is aptly named, for it bears only truth; not even a trace of erroneous knowledge exists therein.
And thus it has been said: 'By scripture, by inference, and by the relish of the practice of meditation—developing wisdom in these three ways, one attains the highest <s>yoga</s>.'
That wisdom moreover—
[Yogasūtra I.49:] has a different object from the wisdom born of scripture and inference, because its object is the particular (<s>viśeṣa</s>).
Scriptural knowledge (<s>śruta</s>) is knowledge from tradition (<s>āgama</s>), and its object is general.
For a particular cannot be conveyed through scripture. Why? Because words are not conventionally established with reference to particulars.
Likewise, inference too has only a general object.
It has been said: 'Where there is connection, there is inference; where there is no connection, there is no inference.'
And through inference, the conclusion is drawn by means of a general property.
Therefore, no particular exists as the object of scripture or inference.
Nor can this subtle, hidden, or remote object be grasped by ordinary perception.

Nor does this particular, which has no other means of knowledge, cease to exist; hence that particular, whether pertaining to the subtle elements or to <s>Puruṣa</s>, is graspable only by the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>.
Therefore, that wisdom has a different object from the wisdom born of scripture and inference, because its object is the particular.
Upon the attainment of the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>, ever-new <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) produced by wisdom arise in the <s>yogī</s>—
[Yogasūtra I.50:] The <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) born from that samādhi obstructs other <s>saṃskāras</s>.
The impression arising from the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s> counteracts the latent deposit of worldly impressions (<s>vyutthāna-saṃskāra</s>).
Due to the overpowering of the worldly impressions, the cognitions arising from them do not occur.
Upon the cessation of those cognitions, <s>samādhi</s> presents itself.
From that arises wisdom born of <s>samādhi</s>; from that arise impressions produced by wisdom—thus an ever-new deposit of impressions is born.
And from that, wisdom; and from that, impressions—and so the cycle continues.
[Objection:] How will this excess of impressions not make the mind further active?
Those impressions produced by wisdom do not make the mind endowed with further activity, because they are the cause of the destruction of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions).
Rather, they withdraw the mind from its own activity.
For the activity of the mind culminates in discriminative knowledge (<s>khyāti</s>).
[Yogasūtra I.51:] Upon the cessation of even that discriminative knowledge, through the cessation of all mental activity, there arises <s>nirbīja samādhi</s> (seedless concentration).
That seedless <s>samādhi</s> is not only opposed to the wisdom of seeded <s>samādhi</s>, but also obstructs even the impressions produced by wisdom.
Why? Because the impression born of cessation (<s>nirodha</s>) counteracts the impressions born of samādhi.
Through the experience of the temporal sequence of the duration of cessation, the existence of impressions created by the mind in the state of cessation is to be inferred.

Together with the impressions conducive to <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) arising from worldly states, cessation, and <s>samādhi</s>, the mind dissolves into its own <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) as it remains established therein.
Therefore, those impressions, being opposed to the continued activity of the mind, do not become causes of its perpetuation.

Since the mind, its function completed, ceases together with the impressions conducive to <s>kaivalya</s>, when it has ceased, <s>Puruṣa</s> remains established in its own essential nature alone—therefore it is said to be pure, absolute (<s>kevala</s>), and liberated.
Thus the <s>yoga</s> of one whose mind is concentrated has been set forth.
How one whose mind is still in the worldly state may also be yoked to <s>yoga</s>—this is now commenced:
[Yogasūtra II.1:] <s>Tapas</s> (austerity), <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study), and <s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s> (devotion to the Lord) constitute <s>Kriyāyoga</s> (the yoga of action).
Without <s>tapas</s> (austerity), <s>yoga</s> does not succeed.

The impurity, variegated by beginningless <s>karma</s>, <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), and <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions), and beset by the net of present sense-objects, does not break down without intense <s>tapas</s> (austerity) — therefore the prescription of <s>tapas</s>.
And that [<s>tapas</s>], which purifies the mind without causing harm, should be practiced through this — so he considers.
<s>Svādhyāya</s> (self-study) is the recitation of purifying [mantras] such as <s>Praṇava</s> (<s>Om</s>) and the like, or the study of scriptures on liberation.
<s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s> (devotion to the Lord) is the dedication of all actions to the Supreme Teacher, or the renunciation of their fruits.
This is <s>kriyāyoga</s>.
Its purpose is the cultivation of <s>samādhi</s> and the attenuation of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions).
This [<s>kriyāyoga</s>], when practiced, cultivates <s>samādhi</s> and attenuates the <s>kleśas</s>.
The attenuated <s>kleśas</s>, rendered like seeds burned by the fire of <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (highest discriminative meditation), incapable of germination — will be made [thus].

From their attenuation, the subtle <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom) — the mere discrimination of the otherness of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> — untouched by the <s>kleśas</s>, having completed its function, will serve for <s>pratiprasava</s> (reabsorption [of <s>Prakṛti</s>]).
Now, what are the <s>kleśas</s>, and how many?
<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance), <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness), <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life) are the <s>kleśas</s>.
The <s>kleśas</s> — these five are called <s>viparyayas</s> (misconceptions), that is the meaning.

When activated, they strengthen the dominion of the <s>guṇas</s>, establish [their] transformation, expand the stream of cause and effect, and, becoming the thread of mutual reinforcement, bring about the fruition of <s>karma</s>.
<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance) is the field of the subsequent ones — the dormant, attenuated, alternating, and active [<s>kleśas</s>].

Here, <s>avidyā</s> is the field, the ground of production, for the subsequent ones — <s>asmitā</s> and the rest — in their four-fold variations of dormant (<s>prasupta</s>), attenuated (<s>tanu</s>), alternating (<s>vicchinna</s>), and active (<s>udāra</s>).
What is dormancy here?
For those that exist only as a potentiality (<s>śaktimātra</s>) in the mind, it is the condition of being in seed-form.
Their awakening (<s>prabodha</s>) is the coming to the forefront when an object-support (<s>ālambana</s>) [appears].

For one who has attained <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (highest discriminative meditation), whose <s>kleśa</s>-seeds have been burned, even when the object-support comes to the forefront, they no longer exist — for a burned seed, whence germination?
Therefore, one whose <s>kleśas</s> are destroyed and who is skilled is called one in the final body (<s>caramadeha</s>).
That very fifth state of the <s>kleśas</s> — the condition of having their seeds burned — exists [only] there [in the perfected <s>yogī</s>], not elsewhere.

The seed-potency of the existing <s>kleśas</s> is then burned; therefore, even when the object comes to the forefront, there is no awakening of these — this is what is meant by the dormancy of those whose seeds are burned and their non-germination.
Attenuation is stated: <s>kleśas</s> that have been assailed by the cultivation of their opposites (<s>pratipakṣabhāvanā</s>) become attenuated.
Likewise, being interrupted again and again, they arise repeatedly with one or another form — these are the alternating [<s>kleśas</s>].
How? Because anger is not seen at the time of attachment.
Anger does not arise at the time of attachment.
And attachment, though seen in regard to one [object], does not not-exist in regard to other objects.

It is not that <s>Caitra</s>, being attached to one woman, is detached in regard to other women; rather, attachment has found its expression [in one], while in regard to others it is a future expression.
For it is then dormant, attenuated, or alternating.
That which has found its expression in [a particular] object is the active (<s>udāra</s>) [<s>kleśa</s>].
All of these do not transcend the domain of the <s>kleśas</s>.
What then is the alternating, dormant, attenuated, or active <s>kleśa</s>? It is said: True indeed is this, but the [designations] alternating and the rest apply only to particular [<s>kleśas</s>].
Just as [a <s>kleśa</s>] ceases through the cultivation of its opposite, so too it is manifested through its own collyrium of expression.
All these <s>kleśas</s> are varieties of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
Why? Because <s>avidyā</s> pervades all of them.
What is produced by <s>avidyā</s> upon an object — the <s>kleśas</s> follow that, are perceived at the time of the erroneous cognition, and as <s>avidyā</s> diminishes, they diminish along with it.
The essential nature of <s>avidyā</s> is now stated:
<s>Avidyā</s> (ignorance) is the cognition of the permanent, pure, pleasurable, and Self in what is impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-Self.
[It is] the cognition of permanence in the impermanent product.
For example: 'The earth is eternal,' 'The sky with its moon and stars is eternal,' 'The celestial beings are immortal.'
Likewise, [the cognition of] purity in the supremely disgusting body—
'From its place [of origin], from the seed, from its support, from its secretions, and also from its final state — the wise know the body as impure, since its cleanliness is [merely] superimposed.'
Thus the cognition of purity in the impure is seen.

'This maiden, beautiful as a crescent moon, as if fashioned from honey and nectar, as if emerged from breaking through the moon, with eyes elongated like blue lotus petals, as if reviving the world of the living with two eyes pregnant with coquetry' — what is anyone's connection with what?
Thus there is the erroneous cognition of purity in the impure.
By this, the cognition of merit in demerit and the cognition of benefit in what is not beneficial are explained.

Likewise, the cognition of pleasure in suffering will be stated: 'From the sufferings of transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>), burning (<s>tāpa</s>), and latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and from the conflict of the activities of the <s>guṇas</s>, everything is indeed suffering for the discriminating one.'
Therein, the cognition of pleasure [in what is suffering] is <s>avidyā</s>.

Likewise, the cognition of Self in the non-Self — whether in external instruments, conscious or unconscious, or in the body as the seat of enjoyment, or in the mind as the instrument of <s>Puruṣa</s> — [all are] the cognition of Self in what is non-Self.

Likewise, this has been said here: 'Having apprehended the manifest or the unmanifest being as Self, one rejoices at its prosperity, thinking it one's own prosperity, and grieves at its adversity, thinking it one's own adversity — such a person is entirely unawakened.'
This four-footed <s>avidyā</s> is the root of this stream of <s>kleśas</s> and of the repository of <s>karma</s> with its fruition.
And the real nature of that [<s>avidyā</s>] is to be understood as being like [the word] 'non-friend' (<s>amitra</s>) or 'non-hoofprint' (<s>agoṣpada</s>).
Just as 'non-friend' (<s>amitra</s>) is not the absence of a friend nor a mere friend, but the opposite of one — a rival (<s>sapatna</s>),
just as 'non-hoofprint' (<s>agoṣpada</s>) is not the absence of a hoofprint nor a mere hoofprint, but a place that is altogether a different thing from both—

so <s>avidyā</s> is not a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), nor the absence of a means of valid knowledge, but a different kind of knowledge opposed to <s>vidyā</s> (true knowledge) — that is <s>avidyā</s>.
<s>Asmitā</s> (I-am-ness) is, as it were, the identity of the power of seeing (<s>dṛk</s>) and the power of being seen (<s>darśana</s>).
<s>Puruṣa</s> is the power of seeing; <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) is the power of being seen. The seeming identity of these two in a single nature is called the <s>kleśa</s> of <s>asmitā</s>.
When the powers of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, which are absolutely distinct and utterly unmixed, seem to attain non-distinction, enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) is imagined.
But upon the recovery of their own true natures, there is only <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) for both — whence then enjoyment?
As has been said: 'One who does not see <s>Puruṣa</s> as distinct from <s>buddhi</s> by form, character, knowledge, and the like, would attribute Self-consciousness to it out of delusion.'
<s>Rāga</s> (attachment) follows pleasure.
For one who has known pleasure, it is the greed, thirst, or covetousness — preceded by the memory of pleasure — toward pleasure or its means; that is <s>rāga</s>.
<s>Dveṣa</s> (aversion) follows suffering.
For one who has known suffering, it is the hostility, anger, desire to harm, or wrath — preceded by the memory of suffering — toward suffering or its means; that is <s>dveṣa</s>.
<s>Abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life), flowing by its own momentum, is deeply rooted even in the wise.
Every living being has this eternal self-wish: 'May I not cease to be! May I continue to exist!'
This self-wish cannot occur in one who has not experienced the nature of death.
Through this [clinging], the experience of previous births is inferred.

This <s>kleśa</s> of <s>abhiniveśa</s>, flowing by its own momentum, seen even in a worm just born — whose fear of death, consisting in the view of annihilation, has not been established by perception, inference, or testimony — implies that the suffering of death has been experienced in previous births.
And just as this <s>kleśa</s> is seen in the extremely deluded, so too it is deeply rooted even in the wise who know the past and the future.
Why? Because the latent impression (<s>vāsanā</s>) arising from the experience of the suffering of death is the same for both the skilled and the unskilled.
These [<s>kleśas</s>], being subtle, are to be overcome by <s>pratiprasava</s> (reabsorption).
These five <s>kleśas</s>, rendered like burned seeds, when the <s>yogī</s>'s function is completed, dissolve into the mind and set along with it.
But for those that remain, having attained seed-form,
their modifications (<s>vṛttis</s>) are to be overcome by <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation).

The gross modifications of the <s>kleśas</s>, attenuated through <s>kriyāyoga</s>, being real, are to be destroyed by <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (highest discriminative meditation, i.e., <s>dhyāna</s>) until they are made subtle, until they are rendered like burned seeds.

Just as the gross dirt of garments is first shaken off, and then the subtle [dirt] is removed by effort and [special] methods, so too the gross modifications of the <s>kleśas</s> have a slight antidote, while the subtle ones require a great antidote.
The repository of <s>karma</s> (<s>karmāśaya</s>), rooted in the <s>kleśas</s>, is to be experienced in the seen (present) or unseen (future) births.
Therein, the repository of meritorious and demeritorious <s>karma</s> arises from desire, greed, delusion, anger, and becoming.
It is to be experienced in the seen (present) birth and in the unseen (future) birth.

Therein, that which is accomplished through intense effort by <s>mantras</s>, <s>tapas</s>, <s>samādhi</s>, or by the worship of the Lord, deities, great <s>ṛṣis</s>, and great beings — that meritorious <s>karmāśaya</s> ripens immediately.

Likewise, injury done again and again with intense <s>kleśas</s> to the frightened, the sick, the destitute, or to those who have come in trust, or to ascetic great beings — that sinful <s>karmāśaya</s> also ripens immediately.
Just as <s>Nandīśvara</s>, a lad, abandoned the human condition and was transformed into an animal.
For those in hell, there is no <s>karmāśaya</s> to be experienced in the seen (present) birth.
For those whose <s>kleśas</s> are destroyed, there is no <s>karmāśaya</s> to be experienced in the unseen (future) birth.
As long as the root exists, its fruition is birth (<s>jāti</s>), lifespan (<s>āyus</s>), and experience (<s>bhoga</s>).
As long as the <s>kleśas</s> exist, the <s>karmāśaya</s> becomes ready to bear fruit; [but] not when the root of the <s>kleśas</s> has been cut off.

Just as rice grains encased in husks, with their seed-potency unburned, are capable of germination, but not when the husks are removed or the seed-potency is burned — so too, the <s>karmāśaya</s> encased in <s>kleśas</s> bears the fruit of fruition, but not when the <s>kleśas</s> have been removed or their seed-potency has been burned by <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>.
And that fruition (<s>vipāka</s>) is threefold: birth (<s>jāti</s>), lifespan (<s>āyus</s>), and experience (<s>bhoga</s>).
Here the following is considered: Is one <s>karma</s> the cause of one birth, or does one <s>karma</s> propel many births?
The second consideration: Does many <s>karma</s> bring about many births, or does many <s>karma</s> bring about one birth?
First, one <s>karma</s> is not the cause of one birth.

Why? Because of the innumerable <s>karma</s> accumulated since beginningless time that remains, together with the present [<s>karma</s>], since there is no fixed order of fruition—despair of the world would follow, and that is undesirable.
Nor is one <s>karma</s> the cause of many births.
Why? Because if, among the many <s>karmas</s>, each single <s>karma</s> were the cause of many births, the remaining [<s>karmas</s>] would have no time for fruition, and that too is undesirable.
Nor does many <s>karma</s> cause many births.
Why? Because those many births cannot occur simultaneously—so [they must occur] in sequence.
And thus the same defect as before [would apply].

Therefore, the accumulation of meritorious and demeritorious <s>karmāśaya</s> (karma-repository), variegated, existing in the state of principal and secondary acquisition, made between one birth and the next death, manifested at death, effecting death by a single impulse, when congealed, produces one birth alone.
And that birth, by that very <s>karma</s>, has its life-span determined.
In that life-span, by that very <s>karma</s>, the experience [of fruition] is accomplished.
That <s>karmāśaya</s> (karma-repository), being the cause of birth, life-span, and experience, is called 'having three fruitions' (<s>trivipāka</s>).
Therefore, the <s>karmāśaya</s> pertaining to one existence has been described.

But that which is to be experienced in the present birth—either initiating one fruition (as the cause of experience), or initiating two fruitions (as the cause of both life-span and experience)—like <s>Nandīśvara</s>, or like <s>Nahuṣa</s>.

But the mind, congealed since beginningless time with <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) produced by the experience of the fruition of afflictions and <s>karma</s>, has been made variegated, as if spread like a fishing-net with knots everywhere—these are the <s>vāsanās</s> going back to many existences.
But this <s>karmāśaya</s> that has been described—this alone pertains to one existence.
Those <s>saṃskāras</s> which are the cause of memory are the <s>vāsanās</s>, and they are from beginningless time.
But this one-existence <s>karmāśaya</s> is of two kinds: of fixed fruition and of unfixed fruition.
Here, this rule applies only to the present-birth-experienceable [<s>karma</s>] of fixed fruition, but not to the unseen-birth-experienceable [<s>karma</s>] of unfixed fruition. Why?
For the unseen-birth-experienceable <s>karma</s> of unfixed fruition has a threefold fate:

Destruction of what has been done but not yet ripened; or subsumption into the principal <s>karma</s>; or long duration of that which has been overwhelmed by <s>karma</s> of fixed fruition and principal [<s>karma</s>].
Among these, the destruction of what has been done but not yet ripened—for example, black (demeritorious) <s>karma</s> is destroyed right here by the arising of white (meritorious) <s>karma</s>.

Where this is stated: 'Two groups of <s>karma</s> are to be known—one heap of sinful <s>karma</s>, the meritorious one destroys [it]. Therefore desire to do good deeds; the seers experience your <s>karma</s> right here.'
Subsumption into the principal <s>karma</s>:
Where this is stated: 'There may be a small mixture, with remedy, with self-examination—[but this is] not sufficient to diminish [the merit] of a skilled person.
Why? Because I have much other merit, into which this has been subsumed; even in heaven it will cause only slight diminishment.'
Or long duration of that which has been overwhelmed by <s>karma</s> of fixed fruition and principal [<s>karma</s>].
How so? It has been stated that death is the common manifesting cause only of unseen-birth-experienceable <s>karma</s> of fixed fruition,
but not of unseen-birth-experienceable <s>karma</s> of unfixed fruition.

But the unseen-birth-experienceable <s>karma</s> of unfixed fruition may be destroyed, or may be subsumed, or may persist for a long time, as long as a common cause that manifests <s>karma</s> does not direct it toward fruition.
Because the place, time, and instrumental cause of its fruition cannot be determined—the course of <s>karma</s> is variegated and difficult to comprehend.
And the exception does not annul the general rule—thus the one-existence <s>karmāśaya</s> is established.
These [<s>karmas</s>] have pleasure and pain as their fruit, due to being caused by merit (<s>puṇya</s>) and demerit (<s>apuṇya</s>). [YS 2.14]
Those—birth, life-span, and experience—caused by merit bear the fruit of pleasure; caused by demerit, they bear the fruit of pain.
And just as this pain is of the nature of what is disagreeable, so even during the time of sense-pleasure there is pain of a disagreeable nature for the <s>yogin</s>.
How so? This is established [as follows]:

Due to the suffering of transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>), burning affliction (<s>tāpa</s>), and latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and due to the conflict of the activities of the <s>guṇas</s>—everything is suffering indeed for the discriminating person (<s>vivekin</s>). [YS 2.15]
Everyone's experience of pleasure is pervaded by attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and depends on conscious and unconscious means—therefore, there exists a <s>karmāśaya</s> born of attachment.
And likewise, one hates the means to pain and is deluded—therefore, there also exists a <s>karmāśaya</s> produced by aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) and delusion (<s>moha</s>).
And it is stated: 'Since enjoyment is not possible without harming beings, there exists a <s>karmāśaya</s> born of violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>) relating to the body.'
And sense-pleasure is said to be <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
That satisfaction and pacification of the senses during enjoyment—that is pleasure.
That non-pacification due to craving—that is pain.
And it is not possible to produce desirelessness in the senses through repeated enjoyment.
Why? Because attachments and the skills of the senses grow in proportion to repeated enjoyment.
Therefore, repeated enjoyment is not the means to [true] happiness.
Indeed, one who seeks happiness and is imbued with sense-objects is like one bitten by a cobra while fleeing from a scorpion's poison—sunk in the great mire of suffering.
This is called the suffering of transformation (<s>pariṇāma-duḥkhatā</s>), which is disagreeable and afflicts the <s>yogin</s> even in the state of pleasure.

Now what is the suffering of burning affliction (<s>tāpa-duḥkhatā</s>)? Everyone's experience of burning affliction is pervaded by aversion and depends on conscious and unconscious means—therefore, there exists a <s>karmāśaya</s> born of aversion.

And one who craves the means to pleasure exerts oneself through body, speech, and mind; thereby one helps and harms others—and through helping and harming others, one accumulates <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>.
That <s>karmāśaya</s> arises from greed and delusion—this is called the suffering of burning affliction.

And what is the suffering of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra-duḥkhatā</s>)? From the experience of pleasure arises a repository of pleasure-impressions; from the experience of pain arises a repository of pain-impressions.
Thus, during the fruition of <s>karma</s>, while experiencing pleasure or pain, there is again an accumulation of the <s>karmāśaya</s>.
Thus this beginningless stream of suffering, having spread forth, distresses the <s>yogin</s> alone, because of its disagreeable nature.
Why? Because the wise person is like an eyeball [in sensitivity].

Just as a thread of wool placed on the eyeball causes pain by its touch but not on other parts of the body, so these sufferings afflict the <s>yogin</s>, who is like an eyeball, but not the ordinary person.

But the ordinary person, abandoning suffering brought by one's own <s>karma</s> as it is experienced, and taking up [more suffering] as it is abandoned—pervaded, as it were, by mental modifications made variegated by beginningless <s>vāsanās</s>, by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) that is to be destroyed, following upon ego-sense (<s>ahaṃkāra</s>) and possessiveness (<s>mamakāra</s>)—is continuously overwhelmed by the threefold afflictions of external, internal, and combined causes, arising one after another.

Thus, seeing the Self and the aggregate of beings carried along by this beginningless stream of suffering, the <s>yogin</s> takes refuge in right knowledge (<s>samyagdarśana</s>) as the cause of the destruction of all suffering.
And due to the conflict of the activities of the <s>guṇas</s>, everything is suffering indeed for the discriminating person.

The qualities of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), whose forms are luminosity (<s>prakhyā</s>), activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), and stability (<s>sthiti</s>), becoming mutually supportive, produce a threefold cognition that is tranquil, violent, or dull.
And the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> is unstable—hence the mind is said to be rapidly changing.
The predominances of form and activity conflict with each other; but the general [aspects] proceed together with the predominances.

Thus these <s>guṇas</s>, with cognitions of pleasure, pain, and delusion acquired through mutual dependence, all become of all forms; but their distinction is made by the predominance of one <s>guṇa</s> over the others.
Therefore, everything is suffering indeed for the discriminating person.
And the origin-seed of this great mass of suffering is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
And right knowledge (<s>samyagdarśana</s>) is the cause of its destruction.
Just as the science of medicine has a fourfold structure—disease, the cause of disease, health, and remedy—
so too: <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration), the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>, <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), and the means to <s>mokṣa</s>.
Therein, <s>saṃsāra</s>, full of suffering, is to be avoided (<s>heya</s>).
The conjunction of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> is the cause of what is to be avoided (<s>heyahetu</s>).
The absolute cessation of that conjunction is avoidance (<s>hāna</s>).
The means of avoidance is right knowledge (<s>samyagdarśana</s>).

Therein, the nature of the one who avoids—it cannot be either something to be adopted or something to be avoided; in avoidance, there would be the fallacy of nihilism (<s>ucchedavāda</s>); in adoption, the fallacy of causation (<s>hetuvāda</s>).
In the rejection of both, [there is] the doctrine of eternalism—this is right knowledge (<s>samyagdarśana</s>).
Thus this teaching is said to have a fourfold structure.
The suffering yet to come is to be avoided (<s>heya</s>). [YS 2.16]
Past suffering, having been passed through by experience, is not in the category of what is to be avoided.
And present suffering, being mounted upon by experience in its own moment, does not become something to be avoided in another moment.
Therefore, only the suffering yet to come—that alone afflicts the <s>yogin</s>, who is like an eyeball, and not the ordinary person.
That alone becomes what is to be avoided.
Therefore, the cause of what alone is declared to be avoidable is pointed out:
The conjunction of the Seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) and the Seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is the cause of what is to be avoided (<s>heyahetu</s>). [YS 2.17]
The Seer is <s>Puruṣa</s>, the experiencer of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect).
The Seen comprises all <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena) mounted upon the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>.

This Seen, like a loadstone, beneficial merely by proximity, becomes an object of perception for <s>Puruṣa</s>, whose nature is seeing, [and who is] its master—having entered the domain of experience and action.
Though having attained its own selfhood through another's nature, though independent in itself, due to serving another's purpose, it is dependent on another.
Of these two—the power of seeing and the power of what is seen—the beginningless conjunction, which is purposeful, is the cause of what is to be abandoned, the cause of suffering—this is the meaning.
And thus it has been said: 'Through the abandonment of the cause of that conjunction, there would be this absolute remedy for suffering.'
Why? Because of perceiving a remedy for what is to be abandoned—the cause of suffering.

Just as: the foot-sole has penetrability, the thorn has the capacity to penetrate, and the avoidance of the thorn is standing on the ground with footwear intervening—whoever in the world knows these three, undertaking a remedy there, does not obtain the suffering born of penetration.
Why? Because of the capacity to apprehend the triad.
Here too, it is <s>sattva</s> alone that is heated by the heating <s>rajas</s>.

Why? Because the action of heating resides in the object; the action of heating is in <s>sattva</s>, in the object—not in the unchanging, actionless <s>kṣetrajña</s> (knower of the field), because [<s>sattva</s>] is the demonstrated object.
But when <s>sattva</s> is being heated, <s>Puruṣa</s> too, conforming to its form, appears to suffer along with it.
The nature of the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is now stated:

[Sūtra:] The seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) has the nature of illumination, activity, and stability; consists of the elements and sense organs; and serves the purposes of experience (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). [YS 2.18]
<s>Sattva</s> has the nature of illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>).
<s>Rajas</s> has the nature of activity (<s>kriyā</s>).
<s>Tamas</s> has the nature of stability (<s>sthiti</s>).

These <s>guṇas</s>, whose divisions are mutually colored [by one another], are transforming, possess the property of conjunction and separation, depend upon one another, have acquired form, and though having the relationship of principal and subordinate parts, have undivided divisions of power—following the distinctions of powers of similar and dissimilar kinds. At the time of dissolution (<s>pradhāna</s>), they show their presence; even in their state as <s>guṇas</s>, their existence is inferred as subsumed within <s>pradhāna</s> through their mere operation; having their capacity directed toward the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>; assisting by mere proximity; like a loadstone; following the activity of one or another without an intervening cognition—they are designated by the word <s>pradhāna</s>.
This is called the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>).
This [seen], consisting of elements and sense organs, transforms in the form of elements—earth and the rest—in both subtle and gross [forms].
Likewise, it transforms in the form of sense organs—hearing and the rest—in both subtle and gross [forms].
