But that is not purposeless; rather, having undertaken a purpose, it proceeds—for the seen serves the purposes of experience and liberation for <s>Puruṣa</s>.

Therein, experience (<s>bhoga</s>) is the ascertainment of the essential nature of desirable and undesirable properties, which has fallen into non-distinction [between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>]; liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) is the ascertainment of the essential nature of the experiencer.
There is no other seeing beyond these two.

And thus it has been said: 'But indeed, in regard to the three <s>guṇas</s> which are agents, and the <s>Puruṣa</s> who is a non-agent, the fourth, of similar and dissimilar kind—the witness of [their] activity—observing all presented existing things brought before [him], does not suspect any other non-seeing.'
These two—experience and liberation—being produced by <s>buddhi</s> and occurring in <s>buddhi</s> alone, how are they attributed to <s>Puruṣa</s>?

Just as victory or defeat, occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the king—for he is the enjoyer of their fruit—so too bondage and liberation, occurring in <s>buddhi</s> alone, are attributed to <s>Puruṣa</s>—for he is the enjoyer of their fruit.
The non-completion of the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> with respect to <s>buddhi</s> alone is bondage; the completion of that purpose is liberation.
By this, grasping, retention, reasoning, counter-reasoning, true knowledge, and tenacity—all occurring in <s>buddhi</s>—have their existence superimposed upon <s>Puruṣa</s>.
For he is the enjoyer of their fruit.
For the purpose of determining the distinctions in the essential nature of the seen <s>guṇas</s>, the following is commenced:
[Sūtra:] The specific (<s>viśeṣa</s>), the non-specific (<s>aviśeṣa</s>), the merely indicated (<s>liṅgamātra</s>), and the unmanifest (<s>aliṅga</s>) are the stages of the <s>guṇas</s>. [YS 2.19]

Therein, space, air, fire, water, and earth are the elements—they are the specific forms (<s>viśeṣas</s>) of the non-specific (<s>aviśeṣa</s>) subtle elements (<s>tanmātras</s>) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

Likewise, hearing, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are the organs of knowledge (<s>buddhīndriyāṇi</s>); speech, hands, feet, excretory organ, and generative organ are the organs of action (<s>karmendriyāṇi</s>); the eleventh, <s>manas</s> (mind), serves all purposes—these are the specific forms of the non-specific characterized by <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness).
This is the sixteen-fold specific transformation of the <s>guṇas</s>.

There are six non-specifics (<s>aviśeṣas</s>). Namely: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell—these are the five non-specifics having one, two, three, four, and five characteristics beginning with sound; and the sixth non-specific is merely <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness).

That which is the merely indicated (<s>liṅgamātra</s>)—the great principle (<s>mahat-tattva</s>)—proximate to the supreme specifics: in that [<s>mahat</s>], in that great self of mere being, having established themselves, they experience the culmination of development.

And when dissolving back, having established themselves in that very great self of mere being, they return to that which is neither being nor non-being, beyond existence and non-existence, without mark, the unmanifest (<s>aliṅga</s>), <s>pradhāna</s> (primal matter).
This is their transformation as the merely indicated (<s>liṅgamātra</s>); and the transformation of the unmanifest (<s>aliṅga</s>) is beyond being and non-being.
In the state of the unmanifest, there is no cause for the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>; the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> is not a cause in the initial state of the unmanifest.
The purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> is not a cause of that [unmanifest state].
That is not made for the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>—thus it is called eternal.
But for the three particular states [of manifestation], the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> is the initial cause.
And that purpose is the efficient cause (<s>hetu</s>), the instrumental cause (<s>nimitta</s>), the cause—thus it is called non-eternal.
The <s>guṇas</s>, which follow all properties, neither set nor arise;
Through their manifestations alone—which have the nature of past and future, of loss and gain, and which follow the <s>guṇas</s>—they appear as if having the property of arising and perishing.
Just as <s>Devadatta</s> becomes poor.
Why? Because his cows die—from the death of the cows alone comes his impoverishment, not from the loss of his own essential nature. This is the equivalent illustration.
The merely indicated (<s>liṅgamātra</s>) is proximate to the unmanifest; therein, what is merged in it is distinguished gradually through progressive transcendence.
Likewise, the six non-specifics, merged in the merely indicated (<s>liṅgamātra</s>), are distinguished due to the fixed order of the sequence of transformation.
Likewise, the elements and sense organs, merged in those non-specifics, are distinguished...
And thus it has been stated before.
Since there is no further category beyond the specifics, the specifics have no transformation into another category.
But their transformations of property, character, and condition will be explained [later].
The seen has been explained; now, for the purpose of determining the essential nature of the seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>), the following is commenced:
[Sūtra:] The seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) is mere seeing (<s>dṛśimātra</s>); though pure, [he] perceives through cognitions. [YS 2.20]
'Mere seeing' (<s>dṛśimātra</s>) means the power of seeing alone, untouched by any qualifying attribute—this is the meaning.
That <s>Puruṣa</s> is neither identical with <s>buddhi</s> nor entirely different from it.
First, he is not identical. Why?
Because <s>buddhi</s> is transforming, having both known and unknown objects.
And its object—whether cows, pots, or the like—being both known and unknown, demonstrates its transforming nature.
But the fact that <s>Puruṣa</s>'s object is always known illuminates his non-transforming nature. Why?

For <s>buddhi</s>, if it were <s>Puruṣa</s>'s object, would have to be both unapprehended and apprehended—[but this is impossible]; therefore it is established that <s>Puruṣa</s>'s object is always known. And from that, his non-transforming nature [follows].
Moreover, <s>buddhi</s> exists for another's purpose, because it acts in combination; <s>Puruṣa</s> exists for his own purpose.
And <s>Puruṣa</s> is the overseer of the <s>guṇas</s>—therefore he is not identical [with <s>buddhi</s>].
Then let him be entirely different.
He is not entirely different. Why?
Because, though pure, he perceives through cognitions.
He perceives the cognition belonging to <s>buddhi</s>; perceiving it, though not of its nature, he appears as if of its nature.

And thus it has been said: 'For the power of the experiencer is non-transforming and non-transferring; yet in the transforming object, as if transferred, it follows its activity. And through the form of <s>buddhi</s> that has attained the semblance of consciousness, its mere imitation of the <s>buddhi</s>-modification—indistinguishable from the <s>buddhi</s>-modification—is called a cognition-modification.'
[Sūtra:] The self of the seen exists for the sake of that [<s>Puruṣa</s>] alone. [YS 2.21]
The self of the seen exists [for <s>Puruṣa</s>].
Its essential nature exists—this is the meaning.
But its essential nature, having obtained its being through another's form, is not seen by <s>Puruṣa</s> when the purposes of experience and liberation have been accomplished.
Through the loss of its essential nature, its destruction is attained—but it does not [actually] perish.
[Sūtra:] Though destroyed for one whose purpose is accomplished, it is not destroyed, being common to others. [YS 2.22]
The seen, though destroyed—having reached destruction—for one <s>Puruṣa</s> whose purpose is accomplished, is not destroyed, being common to other <s>Puruṣas</s>.

Though destroyed for the accomplished <s>Puruṣa</s>, it has not accomplished its purpose for unaccomplished <s>Puruṣas</s>—thus, having fallen into the domain of their seeing, it obtains its own form through another's form.
And therefore, because of the eternality of the powers of seeing and the seen, the beginningless conjunction has been explained.
And thus it has been said: 'From the beginningless conjunction of the property-bearers, there is also beginningless conjunction of mere properties.'
With the intention of describing the nature of conjunction, this sūtra is set forth:
[Sūtra:] Conjunction is the cause of apprehending the essential natures of the owner and the owned. [YS 2.23]
<s>Puruṣa</s> is the owner; conjoined with the seen for the purpose of seeing.
From that conjunction, the apprehension of the seen—that is experience (<s>bhoga</s>).
And the apprehension of the essential nature of the seer—that is liberation (<s>apavarga</s>).
Conjunction ends with the completion of the function of seeing—thus seeing has been stated as the cause of separation.
Seeing is the opposite of non-seeing—thus non-seeing has been stated as the cause of conjunction.
Herein, seeing is not the cause of liberation; rather, from the mere absence of non-seeing there is absence of bondage—that is liberation.
In the presence of seeing, there is destruction of non-seeing which is the cause of bondage—therefore seeing, i.e., knowledge, has been stated as the cause of <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute liberation).

Moreover, what is this 'non-seeing' (<s>adarśana</s>)? Is it the sovereignty of the <s>guṇas</s>? Or is it the non-arising of the principal mind that has displayed its object to the owner whose nature is seeing?
It is the absence of seeing with respect to the seen that exists in oneself.
Is it the purposefulness of the <s>guṇas</s>?
Or is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) the seed of the arising of one's own mind, suppressed along with one's own mind?
Is it the manifestation of the <s>saṃskāras</s> of movement when the <s>saṃskāras</s> of stability are exhausted?
Where this has been stated: <s>pradhāna</s>, existing solely in a state of stability, would become non-<s>pradhāna</s> through not producing modifications.
Likewise, existing solely in a state of movement, it would become non-<s>pradhāna</s> through the perpetuality of modifications.
And in both ways, its activity engages in the operation of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) — not otherwise.
Even when other causes are imagined, the inquiry is the same.
Some say: 'The power of seeing itself is non-seeing,' citing the <s>Śruti</s>: 'The activity of <s>Pradhāna</s> is for the purpose of revealing itself to the Self.'
<s>Puruṣa</s>, capable of knowing all that is to be known, does not see prior to the activity [of Pradhāna]; the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>), capable of all effects and instruments, is then not seen.
Some say that the non-seeing of both is the [essential] property.
Therein, this seeing of the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>), though belonging to its own nature, is dependent on the cognition of <s>Puruṣa</s>, and thus becomes a property of the seen.
Likewise, the non-seeing of <s>Puruṣa</s>, though not belonging to its own nature, dependent on the cognition of the seen, appears as if it were a property of <s>Puruṣa</s>.
Some declare: 'Seeing is knowledge itself; non-seeing [is its absence].'
These are the various interpretations found in the <s>śāstra</s> (scripture).
Therein, this multiplicity of interpretations pertains to the common subject of the conjunction of the <s>guṇas</s> with all <s>Puruṣas</s>.
But as for the conjunction of the individual consciousness with its own intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) —
its cause is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance),
meaning the latent impression of erroneous knowledge (<s>viparyaya-jñāna-vāsanā</s>).

And the intellect, permeated by the latent impression of erroneous knowledge, does not attain the culminating realization of <s>Puruṣa</s> (<s>puruṣakhyāti</s>); having its function still remaining, it returns again.

But when it attains the culminating realization of <s>Puruṣa</s>, its function fulfilled and its seeing of [the conjunction as real] ceased, then due to the absence of the cause of bondage, it does not return again.

Here someone illustrates with the story of the eunuch: a deluded wife says to her husband, the son of a eunuch: 'My sister has offspring — why do I not?' He says to her: 'When I am dead, I shall produce offspring for you.'
Likewise, this knowledge, while existing, does not bring about the cessation of the mind; what hope is there that it will do so when destroyed?
Therein, one who speaks like a teacher says: 'Surely the cessation of the intellect alone is liberation; the cessation of the intellect is due to the absence of the cause of non-seeing.'
And that non-seeing, which is the cause of bondage, ceases through seeing (knowledge).
Therein, the cessation of the mind alone is liberation — why this confusion of mind in an inappropriate matter?

The suffering to be avoided and the cause of what is to be avoided — namely the conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), which has a cause — have been stated. Hereafter, the cessation (<s>hāna</s>) is to be declared.
[Sūtra II.25:] Through the absence of that [ignorance], the absence of conjunction — that is <s>hāna</s> (cessation). That is <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) for the Seer (<s>dṛśi</s>).
[Bhāṣya:] Through the absence of that non-seeing, the absence of the conjunction of <s>buddhi</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, the absolute cessation of bondage — that is the meaning.
This is <s>hāna</s> (cessation).
<s>Kaivalya</s> (liberation) for the Seer — the unmixed state of <s>Puruṣa</s>, meaning non-conjunction with the <s>guṇas</s> once more.
When the cause of suffering ceases, suffering ceases — that is <s>hāna</s>. Then <s>Puruṣa</s> is established in its own nature — as has been stated.
Now, what is the means for attaining <s>hāna</s> (cessation)?
[Sūtra II.26:] Unwavering discriminative discernment (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) is the means to <s>hāna</s> (cessation).
[Bhāṣya:] <s>Vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative discernment) is the awareness of the distinction between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>.
But when false knowledge has not ceased, it [the discernment] wavers.

When false knowledge attains the state of a burnt seed, becoming barren of further production, then the flow of discriminative awareness (<s>viveka-pratyaya-pravāha</s>) becomes stainless for one whose <s>sattva</s> has shaken off the dust of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), who abides in the supreme clarity, in the supreme mastery-consciousness (<s>vaśīkāra-saṃjñā</s>).
That unwavering <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative discernment) is the means to <s>hāna</s>.
Thus, false knowledge attains the state of a burnt seed and ceases to produce again — this is the path to liberation, the means to cessation.
[Sūtra II.27:] For that [<s>yogin</s>], wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) is sevenfold in its final stage.
[Bhāṣya:] 'For that' refers to one of awakened discernment.
'Sevenfold' means: when, through the removal of the impurity-veil of the mind, no other cognition arises, the wisdom of the discriminator is of exactly seven kinds.
Namely: (1) 'What was to be known has been known — there is nothing more to be known.'
(2) 'The causes of what was to be avoided have been diminished — there is nothing more for them to be diminished.'
(3) 'Cessation has been directly realized through <s>nirodha-samādhi</s> (the samādhi of suppression).'
(4) 'The means to cessation, in the form of <s>vivekakhyāti</s>, has been cultivated.'
This fourfold [insight] is the liberation pertaining to wisdom.
But the liberation of the mind is threefold: the intellect whose function is fulfilled.
(5) 'The <s>guṇas</s>, like boulders fallen from a mountain peak, without a resting-place, facing dissolution into their own cause, vanish along with that [mind].'
(6) 'And for these, once dissolved, there is no further arising, due to the absence of purpose.'
(7) 'In this state, <s>Puruṣa</s>, having transcended all connection with the <s>guṇas</s>, is a pure light of its own nature alone, stainless, isolated (<s>kevalin</s>).'
One who perceives this sevenfold wisdom of the final stage is called 'accomplished' (<s>kuśala</s>).
Even upon the involution (<s>pratiprasava</s>) of the mind, the liberated one is called 'accomplished' — because he has transcended the <s>guṇas</s>.
<s>Vivekakhyāti</s> as the means to cessation is established; and the means [to vivekakhyāti] is not accomplished without a further practice — thus [the following] is introduced:
[Sūtra II.28:] From the practice of the limbs of <s>Yoga</s>, upon the destruction of impurity, there arises the light of knowledge, up to <s>vivekakhyāti</s> (discriminative discernment).
[Bhāṣya:] The limbs of <s>Yoga</s> are eight, which will be enumerated.
Through their practice, there is the destruction — the annihilation — of the five-branched error (<s>viparyaya</s>), which is of the form of impurity.
Upon its destruction, the manifestation of right knowledge occurs.
As the practices are performed, impurity progressively becomes attenuated.
And as it diminishes, the light of knowledge also progressively increases, following the order of diminution.
This increase reaches its culmination up to <s>vivekakhyāti</s> — meaning up to the knowledge distinguishing the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>.
The practice of the limbs of <s>Yoga</s> is the cause of the separation from impurity,
just as an axe [is the cause of the separation] of what is to be cut.
But <s>vivekakhyāti</s> is the cause of attainment, just as <s>dharma</s> is the cause of happiness — not a cause in any other way.
How many kinds of causes are there in the <s>śāstra</s>?
Nine only, it is stated.
Namely:
'Production, sustenance, manifestation, modification, cognition, attainment, separation, transformation, and support — causation is remembered as ninefold.'
Therein: the production-cause of cognition is the mind; the sustenance-cause of the mind is its serving the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> — as food is for the body.
The manifestation-cause is as light is for form, so is the knowledge of form; the modification-cause of the mind is a different object —
as fire is for what is to be cooked.
The cognition-cause is the knowledge of smoke for the knowledge of fire.
The attainment-cause of <s>vivekakhyāti</s> is the practice of the limbs of <s>Yoga</s>.
That very same [practice] is the separation-cause of impurity.
The transformation-cause is as a goldsmith is for gold.

Thus, regarding a single cognition of a woman: <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) causes delusion, <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion) causes suffering, <s>rāga</s> (attachment) causes pleasure, knowledge of reality causes equanimity.
The support-cause is the body for the sense-organs,
and those [elements] for that [body].
The great elements are [the support-cause] of bodies; and they [support] each other — among animals, humans, and divine beings — since they serve each other's purposes. Thus there are nine causes.
And these should be applied to other categories as appropriate.
But the practice of the limbs of <s>Yoga</s> obtains causality in only two ways.
Therein, the limbs of <s>Yoga</s> are to be ascertained:

[Sūtra II.29:] <s>Yama</s> (restraint), <s>niyama</s> (observance), <s>āsana</s> (posture), <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control), <s>pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal of senses), <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), and <s>samādhi</s> (absorption) — these are the eight limbs.
We shall describe their practice and nature in order.
Therein:

[Sūtra II.30:] <s>Ahiṃsā</s> (non-violence), <s>satya</s> (truthfulness), <s>asteya</s> (non-stealing), <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy), and <s>aparigraha</s> (non-possessiveness) are the <s>yamas</s> (restraints).
[Bhāṣya:] Therein, <s>ahiṃsā</s> (non-violence) is the absence of hostility toward all living beings, in every way, at all times.
And the subsequent <s>yamas</s> and <s>niyamas</s> are rooted in it and are devoted to its perfection — they are taught for the purpose of establishing it.
They are undertaken for the purpose of making it [<s>ahiṃsā</s>] pure in form.
And thus it is said: 'That <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, as he undertakes more and more vows, turning away from the occasions of violence arising from negligence, makes that very <s>ahiṃsā</s> pure in form.'
[Bhāṣya:] <s>Satya</s> (truthfulness) is [speech and mind] conforming to reality.
As seen and as inferred — so should be the speech and mind.
Speech is uttered for the purpose of communicating one's own knowledge to another; it should be neither deceptive, nor erroneous, nor barren of understanding.
This [truthful speech] operates for the benefit of all beings, not for the injury of beings.

If speech, though uttered in this way, were to be directed toward the injury of beings, it would not be truth — it would be sin. Through such pseudo-merit, a mere resemblance of merit, one would attain miserable darkness.
Therefore, having examined [the situation], one should speak truth that is beneficial to all beings.
[Bhāṣya:] Stealing (<s>steya</s>) is the appropriation of another's property without scriptural authorization; its opposite, in the form of absence of craving, is <s>asteya</s> (non-stealing).
[Bhāṣya:] <s>Brahmacarya</s> (celibacy) is the control of the hidden organ (<s>upastha</s>) of the restrained senses.

[Bhāṣya:] <s>Aparigraha</s> (non-possessiveness) is the non-acceptance [of gifts], seeing the defects of acquisition, preservation, loss, attachment, and injury in objects. These are the <s>yamas</s>.
But these —
[Sūtra II.31:] When not limited by birth, place, time, and circumstance — [they constitute] the universal great vow (<s>mahāvrata</s>).
[Bhāṣya:] Therein, <s>ahiṃsā</s> limited by birth: for a fisherman, violence applies only to fish, not elsewhere.
The same limited by place: 'I will not kill at a sacred pilgrimage site.'
The same limited by time: 'I will not kill on the fourteenth [lunar day], nor on an auspicious day.'
The same, for one who has ceased from the [first] three, limited by circumstance: 'I will kill only for the sake of gods and <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, not otherwise.'
As for <s>Kṣatriyas</s>: violence is only in battle, not elsewhere.
Not limited by these — birth, place, time, and circumstance — <s>ahiṃsā</s> and the rest are to be maintained in every way.
In all domains, regarding all objects, in every way, without any known exception — they are called universal (<s>sārvabhauma</s>), the great vow (<s>mahāvrata</s>).

[Sūtra II.32:] <s>Śauca</s> (cleanliness), <s>saṃtoṣa</s> (contentment), <s>tapas</s> (austerity), <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study), and <s>Īśvara-praṇidhāna</s> (devotion to the Lord) are the <s>niyamas</s> (observances).
[Bhāṣya:] Therein, <s>śauca</s> (cleanliness) — the external [kind] is produced by earth, water, and the like, and by consuming pure food and so on.
The internal [kind] is the washing away of the impurities of the mind.
<s>Saṃtoṣa</s> (contentment) is the absence of desire to acquire more than what is at hand.
<s>Tapas</s> (austerity) is the endurance of pairs of opposites.
The pairs of opposites are: hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, silence of speech and silence of gesture.
And the vows associated with these, as appropriate, are the <s>Kṛcchra</s>, <s>Cāndrāyaṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃtapana</s>, and the like.
<s>Svādhyāya</s> (self-study) is the study of texts on liberation (<s>mokṣaśāstra</s>), or the recitation of <s>Praṇava</s> (<s>Oṃ</s>).
<s>Īśvara-praṇidhāna</s> (devotion to the Lord) is the offering of all actions to that supreme teacher (<s>paramaguru</s>).

Whether resting on bed or seat, or traveling on the road, being healthy, with the web of unwholesome thoughts exhausted, beholding the destruction of the seeds of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), one would be ever-united [with yoga] and a partaker of immortal bliss.
Where this has been said: 'From that [comes] the attainment of inward-directed consciousness and also the absence of obstacles.'
[Sūtra:] When [one is] disturbed by unwholesome thoughts, [one should practice] the cultivation of the opposite.

When unwholesome thoughts such as violence arise in this <s>brāhmaṇa</s> [yogin] — 'I shall kill one who has done nothing wrong,' 'I shall speak falsehood,' 'I shall appropriate his property,' 'I shall have intercourse with his wife,' 'I shall become master of his possessions' —
thus, being afflicted by the blazing fever of thoughts inclined toward the wrong path, one should cultivate their opposites.
'Being roasted in the terrible embers of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), I have taken refuge in the <s>yogadharma</s> (discipline of yoga), which grants fearlessness to all beings.'
'If indeed I, having abandoned [those] unwholesome thoughts, were to take them up again, I would be like one who behaves as a dog' — thus one should contemplate.
'Just as a dog licks up its own vomit, so would I be in taking [them] up again.'
This and similar [reasoning] should be applied in connection with the other <s>sūtras</s> as well.

[Sūtra:] Unwholesome thoughts such as violence — whether done, caused to be done, or approved; preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; mild, moderate, or intense — result in infinite suffering and ignorance. Thus is the cultivation of the opposite.
Therein, violence is first [classified as] threefold: done [by oneself], caused to be done [by another], and approved [when done by another].
Each of these is again threefold: [motivated] by greed — 'for the sake of flesh and skin'; by anger — 'this person has wronged me'; by delusion — 'it will be meritorious for me.'
Greed, anger, and delusion are again each threefold: mild, moderate, and intense.
Thus there are twenty-seven varieties of violence.
The mild, moderate, and intense are again each threefold: mildly mild, moderately mild, and intensely mild.
Likewise: mildly moderate, moderately moderate, and intensely moderate.
Likewise: mildly intense, moderately intense, and supremely intense.
Thus violence has eighty-one varieties.
But further, it is innumerable due to the distinctions of regulation, alternatives, and combinations, since the varieties of living beings are uncountable.
The same should be applied to falsehood and the other [transgressions] as well.
These unwholesome thoughts indeed have infinite suffering and ignorance as their fruit — thus is the cultivation of the opposite.
'Those whose fruit is suffering, ignorance, and endlessness' — thus is the cultivation of the opposite.
And so, the one who does violence first seizes the vitality of the one to be killed.
Then, through the striking of weapons and the like, causes suffering.
Then releases [the victim] even from life.
Through the seizure of vitality, both his conscious and unconscious instruments become depleted of vitality.

Due to producing suffering, he experiences suffering in hells, animal births, ghostly realms, and the like; due to depriving [another] of life, he exists moment by moment on the verge of death, and even when desiring death, barely draws breath because the suffering-fruition must inevitably be experienced.
And if somehow the violence were accompanied by merit [accumulated elsewhere], then in the attainment of happiness, [the perpetrator] would be short-lived.
The same should be applied to falsehood and the other [transgressions] as applicable.
Thus, contemplating this inevitable and undesirable fruition of unwholesome thoughts, one should not fix the mind upon them.

When, through the cultivation of the opposite, the unwholesome thoughts to be abandoned become incapable of producing [further effects], then the mastery arising therefrom becomes an indicator of the yogin's <s>siddhis</s> (attainments).
Namely:
[Sūtra:] When established in non-violence (<s>ahiṃsā</s>), in his presence there is the abandonment of hostility
— among all living beings.
[Sūtra:] When established in truthfulness (<s>satya</s>), actions and their fruits become dependent [on his words].
'May you be righteous' — and one becomes righteous; 'May you attain heaven' — and one attains heaven. His speech becomes infallible.
[Sūtra:] When established in non-stealing (<s>asteya</s>), all jewels present themselves.
Jewels from all directions present themselves to him.
[Sūtra:] When established in celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), there is the acquisition of vitality.
Through its acquisition, one elevates [one's] unimpeded qualities.
And being perfected, one becomes capable of imparting knowledge to disciples.
[Sūtra:] When firmly established in non-possessiveness (<s>aparigraha</s>), there arises the knowledge of the how and wherefore of births.

This [knowledge] arises for him: 'Who was I? How was I? What indeed is this? How indeed is this? What shall we become? How shall we become?' — thus the inquiry into the nature of existence regarding past, future, and present lives presents itself to him of its own accord.
These are the <s>siddhis</s> (attainments) from firmness in the <s>yamas</s> (restraints).
Now we shall speak of the <s>niyamas</s> (observances).
[Sūtra:] From purity (<s>śauca</s>) arises disgust toward one's own body and non-contact with others.
When disgust toward one's own body arises, one practicing purity, seeing the defects of the body and becoming free from attachment to the body, becomes a renunciant.

Moreover, non-contact with others: perceiving the [impure] nature of the body, wishing to abandon even one's own body, and not seeing the body's purity even when washing it with earth, water, and the like — how then would one consort with the extremely impure bodies of others?
Furthermore:
[Sūtra:] And [from purity arise] the purification of <s>sattva</s> (the intellect), cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self.
'Arises' — this completes the sentence.

From purity comes purification of <s>sattva</s>; from that, cheerfulness; from that, one-pointedness; from that, mastery of the senses; and from that comes the fitness of the intellect's <s>sattva</s> for the vision of the Self — this is attained through firmness in purity.
[Sūtra:] From contentment (<s>saṃtoṣa</s>), there is the attainment of unsurpassed happiness.

And thus it has been said: 'Whatever sensual pleasure exists in the world, and whatever great divine happiness — these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the happiness born from the destruction of craving.'
[Sūtra:] Through austerity (<s>tapas</s>), from the destruction of impurities, come perfections of the body and the senses.

Austerity, as it is being practiced, destroys the impurity that constitutes the covering stain. From the removal of that covering stain, perfections of the body such as <s>aṇimā</s> (becoming minute) and others [arise].
Likewise, perfections of the senses [arise], such as hearing and seeing from afar.
[Sūtra:] Through self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>), [there is] communion with the desired deity.
Gods, <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages), and <s>siddhas</s> (perfected ones) come within the vision of one devoted to self-study, and they assist in his endeavors.
[Sūtra:] Through devotion to <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), the perfection of <s>samādhi</s> [is attained].

For one who has surrendered all [one's] being to <s>Īśvara</s>, the perfection of <s>samādhi</s> [arises], through which one knows all that is desired without error — in another place, in another body, and in another time.
Thereby his wisdom knows things as they truly are.

The <s>yamas</s> (restraints) and <s>niyamas</s> (observances) together with their <s>siddhis</s> (attainments) have been described. Now we shall describe <s>āsana</s> (posture) and the rest. Therein:
[Sūtra:] <s>Āsana</s> (posture) is [that which is] steady and comfortable.

Such as <s>padmāsana</s> (lotus posture), <s>bhadrāsana</s> (auspicious posture), <s>svastika</s> (cross-legged posture), <s>daṇḍāsana</s> (staff posture), <s>sopāśraya</s> (supported posture), <s>paryaṅka</s> (couch posture), <s>krauñcaniṣadana</s> (heron-sitting posture), <s>hastiniṣadana</s> (elephant-sitting posture), <s>uṣṭraniṣadana</s> (camel-sitting posture), <s>samasaṃsthāna</s> (even-placed posture), steady-and-comfortable, comfortable-at-will, and others of this kind.
[Sūtra:] [It is perfected] by the relaxation of effort and by <s>samāpatti</s> (absorption) upon the infinite.
'It arises' — this completes the sentence. Through the cessation of effort, the posture is perfected, whereby there is no trembling of the limbs.
Or the mind, absorbed in <s>Ananta</s> (the infinite [serpent]), brings about the perfection of the posture.
[Sūtra:] From that [mastery of posture], there is non-affliction by the pairs of opposites.
Through mastery of posture, one is not overcome by the pairs of opposites such as heat and cold.
[Sūtra:] When that [posture] is achieved, <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control) is the interruption of the movement of inhalation and exhalation.

When posture has been mastered: the drawing in of external air is inhalation (<s>śvāsa</s>); the expulsion of air from the abdominal cavity is exhalation (<s>praśvāsa</s>); the interruption of the movement of both — the absence of both — is <s>prāṇāyāma</s>.
But that [<s>prāṇāyāma</s>]:
[Sūtra:] Having external, internal, and suspended movements, regulated by place, time, and number, it becomes prolonged and subtle.
Where the cessation of movement follows exhalation, that is the external [<s>prāṇāyāma</s>].
Where the cessation of movement follows inhalation, that is the internal [<s>prāṇāyāma</s>].
The third, the suspended movement, is where the absence of both [inhalation and exhalation] occurs at once through a single effort.
Just as water placed on a heated stone contracts on all sides, so [in this third type] both [movements] cease simultaneously.
All three of these are regulated by place — 'this is the extent of its range in terms of place.'
Regulated by time — meaning, delimited by the determination of the number of moments.

Regulated by number — 'with this many inhalations and exhalations [constitutes] the first round; likewise, for one who has been restrained, with this many [constitutes] the second round; and so the third.'
'Thus it is mild, thus moderate, thus intense' — thus is it regulated by number.
This [<s>prāṇāyāma</s>], when thus practiced, becomes prolonged and subtle.
[Sūtra:] The fourth [<s>prāṇāyāma</s>] transcends the domains of external and internal.
Having transcended [the stage] regulated by place, time, and number in the external domain,
likewise having transcended [the stage] regulated in the internal domain,
in both ways it becomes prolonged and subtle.
Preceded by that [practice], through the gradual mastery of stages, the cessation of both movements — that is the fourth <s>prāṇāyāma</s>.
The third, however, is the cessation of movement without reference to domain, occurring once initiated through a single effort, regulated by place, time, and number, becoming prolonged and subtle.

But the fourth — through the determination of the domains of inhalation and exhalation, through the gradual mastery of stages, preceded by the transcendence of both [domains] — is the cessation of movement. This is the fourth <s>prāṇāyāma</s>; this is the distinction [between the third and fourth].
[Sūtra:] From that, the covering of light is diminished.
For this yogin who practices <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, the <s>karma</s> that veils the knowledge of discrimination is diminished.
As they declare:
'With a net of great delusion, having covered <s>sattva</s> (the intellect) whose nature is light, it [<s>karma</s>] yokes it to what ought not be done.'
That <s>karma</s> which covers the light and binds one to <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) becomes weakened through the practice of <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, and diminishes moment by moment.
And thus it has been said:
'There is no austerity higher than <s>prāṇāyāma</s>; from that comes the purification of impurities and the radiance of knowledge.'
Moreover:
[Sūtra:] And there is fitness of the mind for <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration).
Through the practice of <s>prāṇāyāma</s> alone — as stated in the teaching: 'Or by expulsion and retention of <s>prāṇa</s> (breath).'
Now, what is <s>pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal of the senses)?
[Sūtra:] <s>Pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal of the senses) is, as it were, the imitation by the senses of the mind's own nature, when there is disconnection from their respective objects.

In the absence of contact with their respective objects, [the senses follow] as if imitating the mind's own nature; when the mind is restrained, the senses are restrained like the mind and do not require any other means [of control] as do other methods of sense-mastery.
Just as bees follow the queen bee when she flies up and settle when she settles, so the senses are restrained when the mind is restrained — this is <s>pratyāhāra</s>.
[Sūtra:] From that [arises] the supreme mastery over the senses.
Some say: 'Mastery of the senses is the absence of addiction to sound and other [objects].'
'Addiction' (<s>vyasana</s>) means 'affliction' — it casts one away from the good.
Others say: 'Mastery of the senses is knowledge of sound and other [objects] that is unhindered [yet] free from pleasure and pain.'
Through one-pointedness of mind there is simply non-apprehension [of the senses]—so says <s>Jaigīṣavya</s>.

And therefore this is the supreme mastery: that in the cessation of the mind, the arrested senses do not require any separate effort-based means, unlike other [methods of] conquering the senses, for the <s>yogin</s>.
The five external aids [to <s>yoga</s>] have been described.
<s>Dhāraṇā</s> (concentration) is now to be discussed.
<s>Dhāraṇā</s> (concentration) is the binding of the mind to a place. [YS 3.1]

In the navel center (<s>nābhicakra</s>), in the lotus of the heart, in the light in the head, on the tip of the nose, on the tip of the tongue, and in such places, or on an external object—the binding of the mind to a mere modification [at that place] is <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration).
<s>Dhyāna</s> (meditation) is the continuity of cognition directed toward that [object]. [YS 3.2]
In that place, the continuity of cognition directed toward the object of meditation—a homogeneous flow, untouched by any other cognition—is <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation).
That very [meditation], when it shines forth as the object alone, as if empty of its own form, is <s>samādhi</s> (absorption). [YS 3.3]

When meditation itself, though of the nature of cognition, becomes as if empty of its own form, shining forth in the form of the object of meditation alone—due to [the mind's] complete absorption in the nature of the object—then it is called <s>samādhi</s>.
The three together constitute <s>saṃyama</s> (complete discipline). [YS 3.4]
This triad of <s>dhāraṇā</s>, <s>dhyāna</s>, and <s>samādhi</s> together is <s>saṃyama</s>.
These three practices directed toward a single object are called <s>saṃyama</s>.
This is the technical designation in the system (<s>tāntrikī paribhāṣā</s>): '<s>saṃyama</s>' for this triad.
From the mastery of that, the light of wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) [dawns]. [YS 3.5]
From the mastery of that <s>saṃyama</s>, there arises the light of <s>samādhi</s>-wisdom: as <s>saṃyama</s> becomes more firmly established, so does the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s> become more clear.
Its application is by stages. [YS 3.6]
The application of that <s>saṃyama</s> is to the stage immediately following the stage that has been mastered.
For one who has not mastered a lower stage cannot, leaping over the immediately following stage, attain <s>saṃyama</s> on the final stages.
And in the absence of that, how would there be the light of wisdom for him?
But for one who has mastered the higher stages by the grace of <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), <s>saṃyama</s> on lower stages such as knowledge of other minds is not appropriate.
Why? Because the purpose of that [knowledge] has already been understood through other means.
'This is the stage immediately following that stage'—in this matter, <s>yoga</s> itself is the teacher.
How so? For thus it has been said:
'<s>Yoga</s> is to be known through <s>yoga</s>; <s>yoga</s> proceeds from <s>yoga</s>. He who is attentive to <s>yoga</s> delights in <s>yoga</s> for a long time.'
The three [<s>dhāraṇā</s>, <s>dhyāna</s>, <s>samādhi</s>] are inner [limbs] compared to the preceding ones. [YS 3.7]
This triad of <s>dhāraṇā</s>, <s>dhyāna</s>, and <s>samādhi</s> is inner (<s>antaraṅga</s>) to <s>samprajñāta samādhi</s> compared to the preceding five practices beginning with <s>yama</s>.
Even that is external to the seedless [<s>samādhi</s>]. [YS 3.8]
Even that inner triad of practices is external (<s>bahiraṅga</s>) to seedless (<s>nirbīja</s>) <s>yoga</s>. Why? Because [seedless <s>samādhi</s>] exists [only] in their absence.
Now, in the moments of the cessation-mind, since the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> is unstable, what kind of transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) of the mind occurs then?

The <s>nirodha-pariṇāma</s> (transformation of cessation) is [that transformation] associated with the mind in the moment of cessation, [consisting in] the suppression and emergence of the <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence and cessation. [YS 3.9]

The <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence are properties of the mind; they are not of the nature of cognition, so they are not arrested when cognition is arrested. The <s>saṃskāras</s> of cessation are also properties of the mind. The suppression and emergence of these two: the <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence diminish, while the <s>saṃskāras</s> of cessation are deposited.
The moment of cessation pervades the mind—this is the <s>nirodha-pariṇāma</s> (transformation of cessation): the moment-by-moment change in <s>saṃskāras</s> of a single mind.
Then the mind has only <s>saṃskāras</s> remaining—this has been explained in the context of <s>nirodha-samādhi</s> (absorption of cessation).
Its tranquil flow [comes] from <s>saṃskāra</s> (habitual impression). [YS 3.10]
The tranquil flow of the mind depends on the proficiency of the practice of <s>nirodha-saṃskāras</s>.
When those <s>saṃskāras</s> become weak, the <s>nirodha-dharma saṃskāras</s> are overwhelmed by the <s>saṃskāras</s> of the emergence-property.
The <s>samādhi-pariṇāma</s> (transformation of absorption) of the mind is the decline of all-pointedness (<s>sarvārthatā</s>) and the rise of one-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>). [YS 3.11]
All-pointedness (<s>sarvārthatā</s>) is a property of the mind.
One-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>) is also a property of the mind.
The decline of all-pointedness means its disappearance.
The rise of one-pointedness means its manifestation.

The mind pervaded by these two as its properties—this mind, pervaded by these two properties that are its own, namely decline and emergence, becomes absorbed—that is the <s>samādhi-pariṇāma</s> of the mind.
Then again, when the subsided and arisen [cognitions] are similar, [there is] the <s>ekāgratā-pariṇāma</s> (transformation of one-pointedness) of the mind. [YS 3.12]

For the concentrated mind, the preceding cognition has subsided and the subsequent [cognition], similar to it, has arisen; the <s>samādhi</s>-mind is pervaded by both—thus again, without deviation from <s>samādhi</s>.
This indeed is the <s>ekāgratā-pariṇāma</s> of the mind as the substance (<s>dharmin</s>).
By this, the transformations of property (<s>dharma</s>), characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), and state (<s>avasthā</s>) in the elements and sense organs are explained. [YS 3.13]

By this previously described transformation of the mind in the form of property, characteristic, and state—the transformation of property, transformation of characteristic, and transformation of state in the elements and sense organs should be understood.
Therein, the suppression and emergence of emergence and cessation in the substance (<s>dharmin</s>) is the transformation of property (<s>dharma-pariṇāma</s>).
And the transformation of characteristic: cessation has three characteristics, connected with three time-paths (<s>adhvan</s>).
That [cessation], first abandoning the characteristic of the future time-path, without transcending its property-nature, has entered the characteristic of the present,
where there is the manifestation of its own form.
This is its second time-path.
Nor is it separated from the characteristics of the past and the future.

Similarly, emergence, having three characteristics connected with three time-paths, having abandoned the characteristic of the present without transcending its property-nature, has entered the characteristic of the past.
This is its third time-path.
Nor is it separated from the characteristics of the future and the present.
Similarly again, emergence, when coming into being, having abandoned the characteristic of the future without transcending its property-nature, has entered the characteristic of the present,
where, in the presence of the manifestation of its own form, there is activity. This is its second time-path.
Nor is it separated from the characteristics of the past and the future.
Thus again cessation, thus again emergence.
Similarly, the transformation of state (<s>avasthā-pariṇāma</s>): in the moments of cessation, the <s>saṃskāras</s> of cessation become strong, while the <s>saṃskāras</s> of emergence become weak.
This is the transformation of state of the properties (<s>dharmas</s>).

Therein: the transformation of the substance (<s>dharmin</s>) through its properties; the transformation of the properties through the characteristics of the three time-paths; and the transformation of the characteristics through their states.
Thus, the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> does not remain still even for a single moment, [as it undergoes] transformations of property, characteristic, and state.
And the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> is unstable.
The inherent nature of the <s>guṇas</s> has been stated as the cause of activity.
By this, through the distinction of property and substance in the elements and sense organs, the threefold transformation should be understood.
In ultimate reality, however, the transformation is one only.
For a property is nothing but the very nature of the substance; this modification of the substance is elaborated through the door of properties.

Therein, the property existing in the substance undergoes change of state (<s>bhāvānyathātva</s>) in the [three] time-paths—past, future, and present—but not change of substance (<s>dravyānyathātva</s>).
Just as a gold vessel, when broken and reformed, undergoes change of state but the gold does not undergo change.
Another [objector] says: the substance is not different from its properties, because of the non-transcendence of its prior nature;
having fallen into the difference of prior and subsequent states, it would transform through mere immutability (<s>kauṭasthya</s>), if it were a continuous entity.
This is the defect [according to the objector]. Why? Because of the non-acceptance of absoluteness.
This triple world departs from manifestation—because of the negation of permanence.
Even having departed, it exists—because of the negation of destruction.
And from association comes its subtlety; and from subtlety, non-apprehension.

The transformation of characteristic: a property, existing in the [three] time-paths, when present, possessed of the past characteristic, is not separated from the characteristics of the future and the present.
Similarly, when future, possessed of the future characteristic, it is not separated from the characteristics of the present and the past.
Similarly, when present, possessed of the present characteristic, it is not separated from the characteristics of the past and the future.
Just as a man attached to one woman is not therefore dispassionate toward the others.
Here, the objection is raised by others that the transformation of characteristic leads to confusion of the time-paths, because everything possesses all characteristics.
The resolution of this: the property-nature of properties is not something to be established [separately].
And given that property-nature exists, the distinction of characteristics must also be stated—not that the property-nature [exists] only in the present moment.
For in that case, the mind would not have attachment as its property during the time of anger, since attachment is not manifesting then.
Moreover, the three characteristics cannot simultaneously exist in a single manifestation.
But in sequence, the existence of that which has its own manifestation would be [possible].
And it has been stated: the predominances of form and activity conflict with each other, but the general [aspects] proceed together with the predominances.

Therefore there is no confusion. Just as the manifestation of attachment alone occurs somewhere [at a given time], its non-existence elsewhere at that time does not follow; rather, it exists there in its general [form]—so too with characteristics.

The substance (<s>dharmin</s>) is not in three time-paths; but the properties (<s>dharmas</s>) are in three time-paths. Those that are marked and those that are unmarked—among them, those that are marked, attaining such-and-such a state, are designated as 'other' in terms of state, not in terms of substance.
Just as a single digit in the hundreds-place is a hundred, in the tens-place is ten, and in the units-place is one. And just as one and the same woman is called a mother, a daughter, and a sister.
The defect of immutability (<s>kauṭasthya</s>) in the transformation of state has been stated by some.
How so? Because [the property] is separated from the activity of the time-paths.

When a property does not perform its own activity, then it is future; when it performs [its activity], then it is present; when having performed [it], it has ceased, then it is past—thus immutability of both property and substance, of characteristics and states, would follow—so say the objectors.
That is not a defect. Why? Because even when the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) are permanent, there is the variety of their mutual conflict.

Just as configuration, which has a beginning, is merely a property of qualities like sound, etc., which are perishable and destructible, so too the <s>liṅga</s> (subtle body), which has a beginning, is merely a property of the <s>guṇas</s>—<s>sattva</s> and the rest—which are perishable and destructible; and in that, the designation 'modification' [applies].

Here is an illustration: clay as the substance (<s>dharmin</s>), undergoing transformation from one property (<s>dharma</s>)—the form of a lump—to another property, transforms in terms of property into the form of a pot.
The pot-form, having abandoned its future characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), assumes the present characteristic—thus it transforms in terms of characteristic.
The pot, experiencing newness and oldness moment by moment, undergoes transformation of condition (<s>avasthā-pariṇāma</s>).

A different property of the substance is also a condition; a different characteristic of the property is also a condition—thus one single transformation of substance has been shown through differentiation.
Thus it should be applied to other categories as well.
These transformations of property, characteristic, and condition do not transcend the nature of the substance (<s>dharmin</s>)—thus one single transformation encompasses all these distinctions.
Transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) is the cessation of a former property and the arising of another property in an abiding substance.
Therein:
The substance (<s>dharmin</s>) follows the properties that are quiescent, arisen, and indeterminable. [YS 3.14]
A property (<s>dharma</s>) is the capacity of the substance (<s>dharmin</s>) delimited by fitness (<s>yogyatā</s>).
And that [capacity] is inferred from the difference in the production of effects; one [property] is seen as different from another in a single [substance].
Therein, the substance, being present and undergoing its own activity, is distinguished from other properties—those that are quiescent and those that are indeterminable.
But when [a property] is endowed with generality, then, being merely the nature of the substance, how could it be differentiated from what?

Therein, the properties of the substance are quiescent, arisen, and indeterminable. Among these, the quiescent are those whose activity has ceased after having functioned; those with active function are arisen; those immediately following the future characteristic and immediately following the present are past. Why do those immediately following the past not become present? Because the relation of before and after does not apply thus to the past.
Therefore, the past has no immediate successor. Only the future is the immediate successor of the present.
Now, what are the indeterminable? Everything contains the nature of everything (<s>sarvam sarvātmakam</s>).
As it has been stated: in water and earth, the transformative diversity of taste and other qualities is observed in stationary beings.
Similarly, [the qualities] of stationary beings in mobile beings, and of mobile beings in stationary beings—thus, without interruption of species, everything contains the nature of everything.
Due to the constraints of place, time, form, and cause, there is certainly no simultaneous manifestation of all natures.
That which follows these properties—both manifest and unmanifest—having the nature of both universal and particular, is the continuous substance (<s>dharmin</s>).
But for one who holds that there are only properties without a continuous [substance], there would be no experience.
Why? How can one consciousness be appointed as the experiencer of an action performed by another consciousness?
And there would be the absence of memory—for there is no recollection by one [consciousness] of what was seen by another.

And from the recognition of objects, it is established that there is a continuous substance (<s>dharmin</s>) that is recognized as undergoing alteration of properties. Therefore, this is not merely properties without continuity.
Difference in sequence is the cause of difference in transformation. [YS 3.15]
When it is argued that there is only one transformation in a single substance, the difference in sequence becomes the cause of difference in transformation.
For example: clay as powder, clay as lump, clay as pot, clay as shard, clay as particle—this is the sequence.
The property that immediately follows another property—that is its sequence.
The lump ceases, the pot arises—this is the sequence of transformation of property (<s>dharma-pariṇāma</s>).
The sequence of transformation of characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma</s>): the pot's transition from future existence to present existence is the sequence.
Why? Because immediate succession exists where there is a relation of before and after, but that does not exist for the past. Therefore, sequence pertains only to two characteristics.
Likewise, the sequence of transformation of condition (<s>avasthā-pariṇāma</s>): in a new pot, oldness is seen at its end.
And that [oldness], being manifested through a sequence following a succession of moments, reaches full manifestation.
And this third transformation is distinguished from the [transformations of] property and characteristic.
These sequences obtain their own nature when the distinction between property and substance exists.
And a property also becomes a substance in relation to the nature of another property.
But when, in the ultimate sense, non-difference is attributed to the substance, and through that [the substance] itself is designated as the property, then this sequence appears as unity alone.
The properties of the mind (<s>citta</s>) are of two kinds: observable and unobservable.
Among these, those consisting of cognitions are observable; those consisting of mere objective existence are unobservable.
And there are seven of these, whose mere objective existence is established by inference.

'Cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), virtue (<s>dharma</s>), latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>), life-force (<s>jīvana</s>), activity (<s>ceṣṭā</s>), and capacity (<s>śakti</s>)—these are the properties of the mind that are beyond perception.'
Therefore, for the <s>yogin</s> who has gathered all the means, the objects of <s>saṃyama</s> are introduced for the attainment of the desired knowledge:
Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the three transformations, knowledge of the past and future [arises]. [YS 3.16]
Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the transformations of property, characteristic, and condition, knowledge of the past and future arises for <s>yogins</s>.
<s>Saṃyama</s> has been defined as the triad of <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), and <s>samādhi</s> (absorption) upon a single object.
Through that [<s>saṃyama</s>], when the three transformations are directly realized, it produces knowledge of the past and future regarding them.
Due to the mutual superimposition of word, meaning, and cognition, there is confusion; through <s>saṃyama</s> on their distinction, knowledge of the sounds of all beings [arises]. [YS 3.17]
Therein, speech is meaningful only in syllables (<s>varṇa</s>).
And the ear has as its object merely the transformation of sound.
But a word (<s>pada</s>) is grasped by the intellect through the synthesis of sounds.

Since syllables cannot occur simultaneously and have no mutual assistance in their nature, they do not touch, do not establish, and appear and disappear [independently]—thus individually they are said to have a nature that is not a word.

But each individual syllable has the nature of a word, being endowed with the capacity of all designations; appearing as if manifold due to being counterpart to other co-operative syllables; each preceding [syllable] being fixed in a particular [relation] by the succeeding and each succeeding by the preceding—thus these many syllables, following sequence and delimited by conventional association with meaning, these syllables surrounded by the capacity of all designation—the letters 'g', 'au', and <s>visarjanīya</s>—illuminate the meaning of [the word '<s>gauḥ</s>' meaning] that which has a dewlap and so forth.

Thus, of these [syllables] delimited by conventional association with meaning, whose sequence of sounds has been synthesized, that single cognition-appearance—that is the word (<s>pada</s>), the designator conventionally associated with the designated.

That single word, the object of a single cognition, brought about by a single effort, partless, without sequence, without syllables, intellectual, presented by the activity of the cognition of the final syllable—when one wishes to communicate it to another, it is expressed through syllables being uttered, and is apprehended by listeners through worldly cognition permeated by beginningless linguistic behavioral impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), with the understanding as if [already] established.
Its analysis through conventional cognition is: a synthesis of this many [syllables] of this kind is the designator of a single meaning.
Convention (<s>saṃketa</s>), however, has the form of mutual superimposition between word and word-meaning, and is of the nature of memory: 'this word is this meaning; this meaning is this word.'
Thus convention has the form of mutual superimposition.
Thus word, meaning, and cognition are confused due to mutual superimposition: '<s>gauḥ</s>' as the word, '<s>gauḥ</s>' as the meaning, '<s>gauḥ</s>' as the cognition.
One who knows the distinction among these is omniscient.
And in all words there is sentence-capacity: when 'tree' is uttered, 'exists' is understood.
The referent of a word does not deviate from existence.
Likewise, there is no action without an instrument.

And thus, when 'cooks' is uttered, there is an implication of all case-relations; the restatement is for the purpose of specification—the agent, instrument, and object being <s>Caitra</s>, fire, and rice.
And it is observed that word-construction [serves] the sentence-meaning: 'a learned one'—the word—'studies'; 'lives'—'sustains the vital breaths.'
Therein, in the sentence, the word-meaning becomes manifest; from that, the word should be analyzed grammatically as either denoting action or denoting a case-relation.
Otherwise, in cases like '<s>aśvo'japaya</s>' and so forth, due to the similarity of noun and verb [forms], how could what is undetermined be analyzed as either action or case-relation?
The distinction among word, meaning, and cognition [is as follows]:

For example: '<s>śvetate prāsādaḥ</s>'—'the palace shines white'—[this is] the word with action-meaning; '<s>śvetaḥ prāsādaḥ</s>'—'the white palace'—[this is] the word with case-relation meaning; the meaning, which consists of action and case-relation, and the cognition.
Why? Because from the connection 'this is that,' the cognition has a single form—this is convention.
But the meaning 'white' becomes the support (<s>ālambana</s>) of both word and cognition.
For it, undergoing modification through its own conditions, is neither accompanied by word nor accompanied by cognition.
Thus the word, thus the cognition—neither accompanies the other. Therefore, the word is one thing, the meaning another, the cognition another—this is the distinction.
Thus, through <s>saṃyama</s> on their distinction, the <s>yogin</s> attains knowledge of the sounds of all beings.
Through direct perception of latent impressions (<s>saṃskāras</s>), knowledge of previous births [arises]. [YS 3.18]

These <s>saṃskāras</s> are of two kinds: those in the form of <s>vāsanās</s> (impressions), which are causes of memory and afflictions; and those in the form of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, which are causes of fruition (<s>vipāka</s>).
They, being conditioned by previous existences, are unobservable properties of the mind, like transformation, activity, cessation, capacity, and life-force.
<s>Saṃyama</s> on these is capable of producing direct perception of the <s>saṃskāras</s>.
And there is no direct perception of them without the experience of [their] place, time, and cause.
Thus, from the direct perception of <s>saṃskāras</s>, knowledge of previous births arises for the <s>yogin</s>.
Similarly, in the case of others, through the direct perception of [their] <s>saṃskāras</s>, knowledge of others' births [arises].
Here, this narrative is heard:

For the venerable <s>Jaigīṣavya</s>, from the direct perception of <s>saṃskāras</s>, while observing the sequence of the transformation of births across ten great creations, discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>) arose.

Then the venerable <s>Āvaṭhya</s>, subtle-bodied, said to him: 'Having existed through ten great creations with unvanquished <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>, while perceiving the suffering of birth in hells and animal wombs, being born again and again among gods and humans—what more have you found regarding pleasure and pain?'
<s>Jaigīṣavya</s> said to the venerable <s>Āvaṭhya</s>:

'Having existed across the ten great creations, with an intellect-<s>sattva</s> that is unsubdued, perceiving the suffering of birth in the hells and among animals, being born again and again among gods and humans — whatever I have experienced, I recognize all of that as suffering alone.'
The venerable <s>Āvaṭhya</s> spoke:
'This mastery over <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) that your reverence possesses, and this unsurpassed happiness of contentment — is this too placed in the category of suffering?'
The venerable <s>Jaigīṣavya</s> spoke:
'This unsurpassed happiness of contentment is spoken of only in comparison to the happiness of sense-objects.'
'In comparison to the happiness of <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation), it is suffering alone.'

'This property of <s>buddhi-sattva</s> is threefold in its <s>guṇas</s>, and the threefold cognition, placed in the category of what is to be abandoned, is the thread of craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), which is of a painful nature.'
'But from the cessation of the torment of the suffering of craving, this happiness is said to be serene, unimpeded, and entirely agreeable.'
[Sūtra III.19:] Knowledge of another's mind from [<s>saṃyama</s> on] the cognition.
[Bhāṣya:] From <s>saṃyama</s> on the cognition, from the direct perception of the cognition, knowledge of another's mind arises.
But it does not [know] the object supporting that [cognition], because that has not become the object [of the yogin's awareness].
One knows a passionate cognition, but does not know 'it is passionate regarding this particular object.'
The object of another's cognition has not been made the object of the yogin's mind; only the other's cognition itself has become the object of the yogin's mind.
[Sūtra III.21:] From <s>saṃyama</s> on the form of the body, upon the suspension of its power to be grasped, when there is no contact with the light of the eye — invisibility.
[Bhāṣya:] From <s>saṃyama</s> on the form of the body, one suspends the form's graspable power.
When the graspable power is suspended, upon the disconnection of the eye's light — invisibility arises for the <s>yogin</s>.
By this, the disappearance of sound and the rest should be understood as stated.
[Sūtra III.22:] <s>Karma</s> is of two kinds — active (<s>sopakrama</s>) and dormant (<s>nirupakrama</s>). From <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge of death; or from the portents (<s>ariṣṭa</s>).
[Bhāṣya:] <s>Karma</s> that determines the lifespan is of two kinds: active and dormant.
Just as a wet cloth spread out dries in a shorter time — so is the active kind.
And just as that same cloth, bunched up, would dry after a long time — so is the dormant kind.
Or just as fire, released in dry brush, joined with wind from all sides, would burn in a very short time — so is the active kind.
Or just as that same fire, placed gradually on portions of a heap of grass, would burn after a long time — so is the dormant kind.
Then, the <s>karma</s> producing a single lifetime is of two kinds — active and dormant.
From <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge of the final moment — of death.
'Or from the portents' — portents are of three kinds: pertaining to the self (<s>ādhyātmika</s>), pertaining to beings (<s>ādhibhautika</s>), and pertaining to the gods (<s>ādhidaivika</s>).
Therein, the self-portent: one does not hear the inner sound when the ears are closed; or one does not see the light when the eyes are fixed.
Likewise, the being-portent: one sees the messengers of <s>Yama</s> (death); one suddenly sees one's deceased ancestors.
Likewise, the divine portent: one suddenly sees heaven or the accomplished ones (<s>siddhas</s>).
Or everything appears reversed. By these one knows that the final moment has arrived.
[Sūtra III.23:] [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on friendliness and the rest — powers.

[Bhāṣya:] Friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>), compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>), and joy (<s>muditā</s>) — these are three contemplations. Therein, having cultivated friendliness toward happy beings, one obtains the power of friendliness.
Having cultivated compassion toward the suffering, one obtains the power of compassion.
Having cultivated joy toward the virtuous, one obtains the power of joy.
The <s>samādhi</s> that arises from contemplation constitutes <s>saṃyama</s>; from that, powers of unfailing efficacy arise.
Toward the sinful, equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>) is [practiced], but not as a contemplation.
Therefore, there is no <s>samādhi</s> therein, and hence no power arises from equanimity, due to the absence of <s>saṃyama</s>.
[Sūtra III.24:] [From <s>saṃyama</s>] on [various] powers — elephant-power and the like.
[Bhāṣya:] From <s>saṃyama</s> on elephant-power, one obtains elephant-power.
From <s>saṃyama</s> on wind-power, one obtains wind-power — and so on.
[Sūtra III.25:] From directing the luminous activity [of the mind] — knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the distant.
[Bhāṣya:] The luminous (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>) activity of the mind has been mentioned. Directing its light onto an object that is subtle, concealed, or distant, the <s>yogin</s> comprehends that object.
[Sūtra III.26:] From <s>saṃyama</s> on the sun — knowledge of the worlds.
[Bhāṣya:] Their arrangement: the seven worlds.
Therein, from <s>Avīci</s> (the lowest hell) up to the ridge of <s>Meru</s> — this is <s>Bhūrloka</s> (the earth-world).
Beginning from the ridge of <s>Meru</s> up to the pole-star (<s>Dhruva</s>) — the intermediate space-world (<s>Antarikṣaloka</s>), variegated with planets, constellations, and stars.
Beyond that is <s>Svarloka</s> (the heaven-world), fivefold; the <s>Māhendra</s> [world] is the third world.
The fourth is the <s>Prājāpatya</s> [world], <s>Maharloka</s>.
The <s>Brāhma</s> [world] is threefold, namely: <s>Janaloka</s>, <s>Tapoloka</s>, and <s>Satyaloka</s>.
'The <s>Brāhma</s> world has three levels; above that the great <s>Prājāpatya</s>; the <s>Māhendra</s> is called <s>Svar</s>; in heaven are the stars, on earth the creatures.'
This is the summary verse.

Therein, above <s>Avīci</s>, situated one above another, are the six great hell-realms, supported by earth, water, fire, wind, space, and darkness: <s>Mahākāla</s>, <s>Ambarīṣa</s>, <s>Raurava</s>, <s>Mahāraurava</s>, <s>Kālasūtra</s>, and <s>Andhatāmisra</s>.
Where beings, experiencing the suffering earned by their own actions, are born with painful, long lifespans.
Beyond these are the seven netherworlds named <s>Mahātala</s>, <s>Rasātala</s>, <s>Atala</s>, <s>Sutala</s>, <s>Vitala</s>, <s>Talātala</s>, and <s>Pātāla</s>.
This earth is the eighth, the wealth-bearing (<s>vasumatī</s>) with seven continents, at whose center stands <s>Sumeru</s>, the king of mountains, made of gold.
Its peaks are made of silver, <s>vaidūrya</s> (lapis lazuli), crystal, gold, and gems.

Therein, the southern portion of the sky appears dark blue like a blue lotus petal due to the luster of the <s>vaidūrya</s>; the eastern is white; the western is transparent; the northern is like a <s>kuraṇṭaka</s> flower.
On its southern side is the <s>Jambu</s> tree, from which this <s>Jambūdvīpa</s> [takes its name].
Due to the course of the sun, day and night proceed as if attached.
To the north are three mountains — <s>Nīla</s>, <s>Śveta</s>, and <s>Śṛṅgavat</s> — each two thousand <s>yojanas</s> in length.
Between them are three regions, each nine thousand <s>yojanas</s>: <s>Ramaṇaka</s>, <s>Hiraṇmaya</s>, and <s>Uttarakuru</s>.
To the south, <s>Niṣedha</s>, <s>Hemakūṭa</s>, and <s>Himāśaila</s> (the Himalayas), each two thousand <s>yojanas</s> in length.
Between them are three regions, each nine thousand <s>yojanas</s>: <s>Harivarṣa</s>, <s>Kimpuruṣa</s>, and <s>Bhārata</s>.
East of <s>Sumeru</s> are <s>Bhadrāśva</s> with <s>Mālyavat</s> as its boundary; west are <s>Ketumāla</s> with <s>Gandhamādana</s> as its boundary.
In the center is the region of <s>Ilāvṛta</s>. This <s>Jambūdvīpa</s> is a hundred thousand <s>yojanas</s>, extended by half that distance in each direction from <s>Sumeru</s>.
This <s>Jambūdvīpa</s>, a hundred thousand <s>yojanas</s> in extent, is encircled by the ring-shaped salt ocean, twice its size.

Beyond that, each twice the previous, are the continents of <s>Śāka</s>, <s>Kuśa</s>, <s>Krauñca</s>, <s>Śālmala</s>, <s>Gomeda</s> (<s>Plakṣa</s>), and <s>Puṣkara</s>; and the oceans, paired like mustard seeds, adorned with various mountains, [filled with] sugarcane juice, wine, ghee, yogurt whey, milk, and fresh water.
Seven [continents], encircled by the oceans, ring-shaped, bordered by the <s>Lokāloka</s> mountain, totaling fifty <s>koṭi</s> <s>yojanas</s>.
All of this is arranged within the well-established cosmic egg (<s>aṇḍa</s>).
And the egg is a minute particle of <s>Pradhāna</s> — like a firefly in space.

Therein, in the netherworlds, in the oceans, and in the mountains, reside the divine groups: <s>Asuras</s>, <s>Gandharvas</s>, <s>Kinnaras</s>, <s>Kimpuruṣas</s>, <s>Yakṣas</s>, <s>Rākṣasas</s>, <s>Bhūtas</s>, <s>Pretas</s>, <s>Piśācas</s>, <s>Apasmārakas</s>, <s>Apsarases</s>, <s>Brahma-rākṣasas</s>, <s>Kūṣmāṇḍas</s>, and <s>Vināyakas</s>.
On all the continents dwell meritorious beings — divine humans.
<s>Sumeru</s> is the garden-ground of the gods. There are the gardens: <s>Miśravana</s>, <s>Nandana</s>, <s>Caitraratha</s>, and <s>Sumānasa</s>.
<s>Sudharmā</s> is the divine assembly; <s>Sudarśana</s> is the city; <s>Vaijayanta</s> is the palace.

The planets, constellations, and stars, bound to <s>Dhruva</s> (the pole-star), with their courses regulated by the restraint of the wind, situated one above another above <s>Sumeru</s>, revolve in the sky.

The six divine groups dwelling in the <s>Māhendra</s> [world] are: the <s>Tridaśas</s>, <s>Agniṣvāttas</s>, <s>Yāmyas</s>, <s>Tuṣitas</s>, <s>Aparinirmitavaśavartins</s>, and <s>Parinirmitavaśavartins</s>.

All possess wish-fulfilling powers, endowed with lordly powers such as <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness) and the rest, celestial in lifespan, <s>Vṛndārakas</s>, enjoyers of pleasures, with bodies born spontaneously, served by excellent and agreeable <s>Apsarases</s>.
In the great <s>Maharloka</s>, the <s>Prājāpatya</s> [world], there are five divine groups: <s>Kumudas</s>, <s>Ṛbhavas</s>, <s>Pratardanas</s>, <s>Añjanābhas</s>, and <s>Pracitābhas</s>.
These have mastery over the great elements, feed on meditation, and have lifespans of a thousand <s>kalpas</s>.
In the first <s>Brāhma</s> [world], <s>Janaloka</s>, there are four divine groups: <s>Brahmapurohitas</s>, <s>Brahmakāyikas</s>, <s>Brahmamahākāyikas</s>, and <s>Amaras</s>.
These have mastery over the elements and senses, with lifespans each doubling the previous.
In the second [<s>Brāhma</s> world], <s>Tapoloka</s>, there are three divine groups: <s>Ābhāsvaras</s>, <s>Mahābhāsvaras</s>, and <s>Satyamahābhāsvaras</s>.

These have mastery over elements, senses, and <s>Prakṛti</s>, with lifespans each doubling the previous, feeding on meditation, with upward-directed seed, with unobstructed knowledge above and knowledge unrestricted regarding the lower realms.

In the third <s>Brāhma</s> [world], <s>Satyaloka</s>, there are four divine groups, dwelling not in constructed abodes but self-established, stationed one above another, with mastery over <s>Pradhāna</s>, with lifespans extending to the duration of creation.

Therein, the <s>Acyutas</s> (the Unfallen) have the bliss of meditation with deliberation (<s>savitarka</s>); the <s>Śuddhanivāsas</s> (Pure Abodes) have the bliss of meditation with reflection (<s>savicāra</s>); the <s>Satyābhas</s> (True Radiances) have the bliss of meditation as pure bliss (<s>ānandamātra</s>); and the <s>Saṃjñāsaṃjñins</s> (Conscious-and-Semi-conscious) have the bliss of meditation as mere I-am-ness (<s>asmitāmātra</s>).
Even they, however, take their stand within the three worlds.
These seven worlds are all indeed <s>Brahma</s>-worlds.
But the <s>Videhas</s> (bodiless ones) and those absorbed in <s>Prakṛti</s> (<s>prakṛtilayas</s>) abide in the state of liberation — they are not placed within the worlds.

This is to be directly perceived by the <s>yogin</s>, having made the beginning through the gateway of the sun; and then elsewhere too, one should practice in this way until all of this has been seen.
[Sūtra III.27:] From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the moon — knowledge of the arrangement of the stars.
[Bhāṣya:] Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the moon, one should know the arrangement of the stars.
[Sūtra III.28:] From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on <s>Dhruva</s> (the pole-star) — knowledge of their motion.
[Bhāṣya:] Then, having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on <s>Dhruva</s>, one should know the motion of the stars. Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the celestial vehicles above, one should know them.
[Sūtra III.29:] From [<s>saṃyama</s>] on the navel center — knowledge of the arrangement of the body.

[Bhāṣya:] Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the navel center (<s>nābhicakra</s>), one should know the arrangement of the body. The three <s>doṣas</s> (humors) are <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>śleṣma</s> (phlegm).
The seven <s>dhātus</s> (bodily constituents) are: skin, blood, flesh, sinew, bone, marrow, and reproductive fluid. Each preceding one is more external — this is their arrangement.
[Yogasūtra III.30:] By <s>saṃyama</s> (concentrated discipline) on the throat-pit (<s>kaṇṭhakūpa</s>), the cessation of hunger and thirst.
Below the tongue is the soft palate (<s>tantu</s>), below that is the throat, and below that is the pit (<s>kūpa</s>). By <s>saṃyama</s> there, hunger and thirst do not afflict one.
[Yogasūtra III.31:] By <s>saṃyama</s> on the <s>kūrma-nāḍī</s> (tortoise channel), steadiness.
Below the pit, in the chest, there is a channel in the shape of a tortoise. Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on it, one attains a steady posture—like a serpent or a monitor lizard.
[Yogasūtra III.32:] By <s>saṃyama</s> on the light at the crown of the head, the vision of <s>siddhas</s> (perfected beings).
Inside the opening in the skull of the head, there is a radiant light. Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> there, one gains the vision of <s>siddhas</s> who move in the space between heaven and earth.
[Yogasūtra III.33:] Or, through <s>prātibha</s> (intuitive knowledge), all knowledge arises.

<s>Prātibha</s> is the intuitive flash called <s>tāraka</s> (liberating), which is the precursor of the knowledge born from discrimination (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>)—like the dawn-glow preceding the rising of the sun. Through that, the <s>yogī</s> knows everything upon the arising of intuitive knowledge.
[Yogasūtra III.34:] By <s>saṃyama</s> on the heart, knowledge of the mind (<s>citta</s>).
In this city of <s>Brahman</s> (<s>brahmapura</s>), there is a small lotus-like dwelling—therein resides consciousness. By <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge of the mind arises.

[Yogasūtra III.35:] Experience (<s>bhoga</s>) is a cognition that does not distinguish between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, which are absolutely distinct. By <s>saṃyama</s> on the Self's own purpose, as distinct from another's purpose, knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s> arises.

The <s>buddhi-sattva</s> (luminous essence of the intellect), whose nature is illumination, having subdued <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>—which are bound to the same <s>sattva</s>—is transformed into the cognition of the distinction between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>.
And from that <s>sattva</s>, which is subject to transformation, <s>Puruṣa</s> is absolutely different in nature—pure, other, of the nature of pure consciousness alone.

Of these two, which are absolutely unmixed, the undifferentiated cognition is experience (<s>bhoga</s>), since experience has <s>Puruṣa</s> as its presented object. That experiential cognition is a visible modification of <s>sattva</s>, since <s>sattva</s> exists for another's purpose.

But that which is distinct from it, of the nature of pure consciousness alone, the other—the cognition pertaining to <s>Puruṣa</s>—by <s>saṃyama</s> on that, wisdom whose object is <s>Puruṣa</s> arises.

And <s>Puruṣa</s> is not seen through the cognition pertaining to <s>Puruṣa</s>, which is of the nature of <s>buddhi-sattva</s>. <s>Puruṣa</s> alone sees that cognition, which rests upon its own Self. As it has been said: 'By what, O dear one, should one know the knower?' [<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad</s> 2.4.14]

[Yogasūtra III.36:] From that arise <s>prātibha</s> (intuition), <s>śrāvaṇa</s> (divine hearing), <s>vedanā</s> (divine touch), <s>ādarśa</s> (divine sight), <s>āsvāda</s> (divine taste), and <s>vārtā</s> (divine smell).
From <s>prātibha</s> (intuition): knowledge of the subtle, hidden, remote, past, and future.
