From <s>śrāvaṇa</s>: the hearing of divine sounds. From <s>vedanā</s>: the attainment of divine touch.
From <s>ādarśa</s>: knowledge of divine forms. From <s>āsvāda</s>: knowledge of divine tastes. From <s>vārtā</s>: knowledge of divine smells. These arise constantly.
[Yogasūtra III.37:] These are obstacles to <s>samādhi</s>, but powers (<s>siddhis</s>) in the worldly state.

These—<s>prātibha</s> and the rest—arising in one whose mind is concentrated, are obstacles since they are opposed to the vision of truth. But arising in one whose mind is in the worldly state, they are <s>siddhis</s> (powers).
[Yogasūtra III.38:] Through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the knowledge of the passages of the mind, there arises the entry into another's body.

The mind, having become worldly, is bound to the body—established there—under the power of the <s>karmāśaya</s> (reservoir of karmic impressions). This is the meaning: its binding to the body. The loosening of that <s>karma</s>, which is the cause of bondage, occurs through the power of <s>samādhi</s>.

And the knowledge of the passages of the mind is also born of <s>samādhi</s>. Through the destruction of karmic bondage and through the knowledge of the passages of one's own mind, the <s>yogī</s> withdraws the mind from his own body and places it in other bodies.
When the mind is placed in another body, the senses follow after it.
Just as bees follow the king-bee when it flies up and settle when it settles, so too the senses conform to the mind when entering another's body.
[Yogasūtra III.39:] Through mastery of <s>udāna</s>, there is non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and the like, and the power of ascension.
Life is the total activity of the senses, characterized by <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest. Its action is fivefold: <s>prāṇa</s> is the movement through the mouth and nostrils, functioning up to the heart.
<s>Samāna</s>, so called because it leads equally, functions at the navel.
<s>Apāna</s>, so called because it leads away, functions down to the soles of the feet. <s>Udāna</s>, so called because it leads upward, functions up to the head. <s>Vyāna</s> is all-pervading.

Among these, <s>prāṇa</s> is the chief. Through mastery of <s>udāna</s>, there is non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and the like; and ascension occurs at the time of death. One attains this through mastery.
[Yogasūtra III.40:] Through mastery of <s>samāna</s>, blazing radiance.
Having mastered <s>samāna</s> and fanning the fire of the body, one blazes with radiance.
[Yogasūtra III.41:] Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the relation between the ear and space, divine hearing.
Space is the basis of all ears and of all sounds. As it has been said: 'For those hearing from the same location, there is a single hearing for all.' And this is the mark of space.
And it has been said to be unobstructable. Since the formless is seen to be unobstructable, the all-pervasiveness of space is also well-known.
The ear is inferred from the apprehension of sound.

Between a deaf and a non-deaf person, one apprehends sound while the other does not. Therefore, it is the ear alone that has sound as its object. For the <s>yogī</s> who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the relation between the ear and space, divine hearing arises.
[Yogasūtra III.42:] Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the relation between the body and space, and through absorption into light things like cotton, movement through space.

Wherever the body is, there is space; since space gives room to the body, the body has a connection with it. Having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on that connection and having mastered it, or having obtained absorption into light things such as cotton down to atoms, having mastered the connection, one becomes light.
And through lightness, one walks on water with one's feet. Then, having traveled on a spider's web thread, one travels on rays of light. Then, movement through space at will becomes possible.
[Yogasūtra III.43:] The unimagined external mental activity is the <s>mahāvidehā</s> (great bodiless state); from that, the covering of light is destroyed.

The concentration (<s>dhāraṇā</s>) called <s>videhā</s> (bodiless) is the gaining of mental activity outside the body. If that occurs merely as an external activity of the mind still established in the body, it is called 'imagined' (<s>kalpitā</s>).

But that external mental activity which belongs to the mind that has actually gone outside, independent of the body—that is 'unimagined' (<s>akalpitā</s>). Through the imagined, one achieves the unimagined—the <s>mahāvidehā</s> (great bodiless state).

Through which <s>yogīs</s> enter other bodies. And from that concentration, the covering of the <s>buddhi-sattva</s> whose nature is illumination—namely, the threefold covering of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s>, and <s>vipāka</s> (karmic fruition), rooted in <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>—is destroyed.
[Yogasūtra III.44:] Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the gross, essential nature, subtle, inherent, and purposeful aspects of the elements, mastery over the elements (<s>bhūtajaya</s>).

Therein, the specific modifications of earth and the rest—sound and the other tanmātras—together with properties such as form and the like, are designated by the term 'gross.' This is the first aspect of the elements.

The second aspect is their common essential nature: solidity is earth, cohesion is water, heat is fire, impulsion and omnidirectional motion is wind, space—this is expressed by the term 'essential nature' (<s>svarūpa</s>).
Of this common nature, the specific modifications are sound and the rest. And thus it has been said: 'Among those endowed with a single class, the distinction is by properties alone.'

Here, substance (<s>dravya</s>) is the aggregate of general and specific properties. For a composite is twofold: that in which the distinction of parts has receded—such as a body, a tree, a herd, a forest.

By the word substance, the aggregate in which the distinction of parts is retained is also meant—of both kinds are gods and humans. Gods are one part of the aggregate, humans the second—the aggregate is denoted by both.
And it is expressed with respect to both distinction and non-distinction: 'a grove of mangoes,' 'an assembly of <s>brāhmaṇas</s>'—'a mango grove,' 'a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> assembly.'
And this is twofold: having separable parts (<s>yutasiddha</s>) and having inseparable parts (<s>ayutasiddha</s>).
A composite with separable parts: a forest, an assembly. A composite with inseparable parts: a compound body, a tree, an atom.
A composite in which the distinction of inseparable parts is present is substance (<s>dravya</s>)—so says <s>Patañjali</s>. This has been called 'essential nature.'

Now, what is their subtle aspect? The <s>tanmātra</s> is the cause of the elements; its single part is the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>)—an aggregate in which the distinction of inseparable parts, consisting of general and specific properties, is present. Thus all the <s>tanmātras</s>—this is the third aspect.

Now, the fourth aspect of the elements: the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities), whose nature is illumination (<s>khyāti</s>), activity (<s>kriyā</s>), and stability (<s>sthiti</s>), which follow the nature of their effects—these are expressed by the term 'inherent' (<s>anvaya</s>).

Now, the fifth aspect is purposefulness (<s>arthavatva</s>): the purpose of experience (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) is inherent in the <s>guṇas</s>; and the <s>guṇas</s> are inherent in the <s>tanmātras</s>, elements, and products—therefore everything is purposeful.
Now, by performing <s>saṃyama</s> on these five elements in their five aspects, the vision of the essential nature of each aspect and mastery over it manifests.

Therein, having conquered the five essential natures of the elements, one becomes a master of the elements (<s>bhūtajayī</s>). Through that mastery, the elemental natures become obedient to one's will, like cows following their calves.
[Yogasūtra III.45:] From that mastery arise the manifestation of <s>aṇimā</s> and other powers, perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by the properties of the elements.
Therein: through <s>aṇimā</s>, one becomes minute; through <s>laghimā</s>, one becomes light; through <s>mahimā</s>, one becomes great.

Through <s>prāpti</s> (extension), even with the tip of a finger one touches the moon. <s>Prākāmya</s> (irresistible will) is the non-obstruction of desire—one rises and sinks in the earth as in water.

Through <s>vaśitva</s> (mastery), one has command over elements and their products, and is not under the command of others. Through <s>īśitṛtva</s> (lordship), one governs their origination, dissolution, and arrangement.

<s>Yatrakāmāvasāyitva</s> (fulfillment of every resolve) is the truthfulness of will—as one resolves, so the elemental natures abide. Yet even one who is capable does not reverse the nature of things. Why? Because of the resolve of another <s>yatrakāmāvasāyin</s> who has attained perfection earlier regarding those very elements. These are the eight sovereign powers (<s>aiśvaryas</s>).

Perfection of the body will be described. And non-obstruction by the properties of the elements: earth with its solidity does not obstruct the bodily and other activities of the <s>yogī</s>—he enters even into rock.

Water with its moisture does not wet him. Fire with its heat does not burn him. Wind with its impulsion does not carry him away. Even in space, whose nature is non-obstruction, his body becomes concealed—he becomes invisible even to <s>siddhas</s> (perfected beings).
[Yogasūtra III.46:] Beauty of form, gracefulness, strength, and diamond-like hardness constitute perfection of the body (<s>kāyasampat</s>).
One becomes beautiful, radiant, of extraordinary strength, and of diamond-like compactness.
[Yogasūtra III.47:] Through <s>saṃyama</s> on the grasping, essential nature, I-sense, inherent, and purposeful aspects, mastery over the senses (<s>indriyajaya</s>).

The object of cognition, consisting of general and specific properties, is sound and the like. The activity of the senses in regard to these is 'grasping' (<s>grahaṇa</s>). But one might ask: if the form of grasping is merely of the general, how could that specific object, not yet examined, be determined by the sense organ through the mind?

The essential nature, however: the sense organ (<s>indriya</s>) is a substance—a composite in which the distinction of inseparable parts of the general and specific properties is present—of the <s>buddhi-sattva</s> whose nature is illumination.
Their third aspect is <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-principle), characterized by <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness).

Of that general [substance], the senses are the particulars. The fourth form: the <s>guṇas</s>, whose nature is illumination, activity, and stability, are purposive in character; the senses, together with <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-sense), undergo transformation.
The fifth form: that which, following the <s>guṇas</s>, constitutes their having-the-purpose-of-<s>Puruṣa</s> (<s>puruṣārthavatva</s>).

In these five forms of the senses, <s>saṃyama</s> (complete restraint) performed in order on each one, having achieved mastery in each, from the mastery of the five forms, mastery of the senses manifests for the <s>yogin</s>.
From that, swiftness of mind, freedom from the instruments [of sense], and mastery over <s>Pradhāna</s> (primal matter).

Swiftness of mind (<s>manojavitva</s>): the body attains unsurpassed speed of movement. Freedom from the instruments (<s>vikaraṇabhāva</s>): the disembodied senses function in accordance with the desired place, time, and object.

Mastery over all modifications of <s>Prakṛti</s> is mastery over <s>Pradhāna</s>. These three <s>siddhis</s> (attainments) are called <s>madhupratīkā</s> ('honey-faced'). And these are attained through mastery of the five forms of the instruments.
For one who has merely the discernment of the distinction between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> (<s>sattvapuruṣānyatākhyāti</s>), there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience.

For one whose <s>buddhi-sattva</s> (intellect-purity) has cast off the impurity of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, who abides in the supreme <s>vaiśāradya</s> (clarity), in the supreme <s>vaśīkāra-saṃjñā</s> (mastery-awareness), who is established in the form of mere discernment of the distinction between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>—sovereignty over all states of existence.

All the <s>guṇas</s>, being of the nature of the purposive and the purpose-served, stand before their master, the <s>kṣetrajña</s> (field-knower), with their entire visible nature—this is the meaning.

Omniscience (<s>sarvajñātṛtva</s>): the discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>) that arises without sequence regarding all <s>guṇas</s> established in the dharma-nature of the quiescent, arisen, and indeterminable—this is the meaning.

This is the <s>siddhi</s> (attainment) called <s>viśokā</s> ('free from sorrow'), having attained which the <s>yogin</s>, omniscient, with the bonds of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) destroyed, abides as master.
From dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) even toward that, with the destruction of the seed of defects, <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute liberation).

When he has this [understanding]: 'This discriminative cognition is the <s>dharma</s> of <s>sattva</s>, when <s>kleśas</s> and <s>karmas</s> have been destroyed; and <s>sattva</s> is placed in the category to be abandoned; and <s>Puruṣa</s> is non-transforming, pure, other than <s>sattva</s>.'
Thus, for him becoming dispassionate, the seeds of <s>kleśas</s>, like roasted rice-seeds incapable of sprouting, together with the mind, proceed toward dissolution.
When these have dissolved, <s>Puruṣa</s> no longer experiences this threefold suffering (<s>tāpatraya</s>).

When these <s>guṇas</s>, manifested in the mind through the nature of <s>karma</s>, <s>kleśas</s>, and fruition (<s>vipāka</s>), having fulfilled their purpose, undergo involution (<s>pratiprasava</s>)—the absolute separation of <s>Puruṣa</s> from the <s>guṇas</s> is <s>kaivalya</s>. Then the power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>) abides in its own form—that alone is <s>Puruṣa</s>.
Upon being invited by those occupying celestial stations (<s>sthānins</s>), one should not form attachment or pride, for there would be recurrence of the undesirable.

There are indeed four types of <s>yogins</s>: the <s>prāthamakalpika</s> (beginner), the <s>madhubhūmika</s> (one on the honey-stage), the <s>prajñājyotis</s> (one whose light is wisdom), and the <s>atikrāntabhāvanīya</s> (one who has transcended what is to be cultivated).

Among them, the first is the practitioner (<s>abhyāsī</s>) whose light of practice has merely begun. The second has <s>ṛtambharā prajñā</s> (truth-bearing wisdom). The third has conquered the elements and senses. Having made protective bonds regarding all things to be cultivated, [he is freed] from the means still to be accomplished.
The fourth, who has transcended what is to be cultivated—for him, the dissolution of mind is the sole purpose. His wisdom is the sevenfold wisdom of the final stage (<s>prāntabhūmiprajñā</s>).

There, the celestial beings of the stations, seeing the purity of <s>sattva</s> in the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> who directly perceives the honey-like stage (<s>madhumatī bhūmi</s>), invite him with their stations: 'Sir, sit here, delight here; this enjoyment is delightful, this maiden is charming; this elixir (<s>rasāyana</s>) wards off old age and death; this is an aerial vehicle; these are wish-fulfilling trees (<s>kalpadrumas</s>); this is the sacred <s>Mandākinī</s>; these accomplished great sages are excellent; the celestial nymphs (<s>apsaras</s>) are favorable; with divine hearing and sight; the body is like a diamond (<s>vajra</s>); all this has been earned by your own merits; O long-lived one, accept this imperishable, ageless, deathless abode, dear to the gods.'

Being thus addressed, he should contemplate the defects of attachment: 'Having been roasted in the terrible embers of <s>saṃsāra</s>, revolving in the darkness of birth and death, I have somehow found this lamp of <s>yoga</s> that destroys the darkness of <s>kleśas</s>; and these sense-objects, propelled by the wind of craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), are its adversaries.'
'Having obtained the light, how could I, deceived by this mirage of sense-objects, make myself fuel for that very blazing fire of <s>saṃsāra</s> again?'
'Farewell to you, O sense-objects, dreamlike and sought after by the wretched'—with such resolved mind, he should cultivate <s>samādhi</s>.

Not having formed attachment, he should also not feel pride, thinking 'I am sought after even by the gods.' From pride, thinking himself well-established, he will not contemplate himself as if seized by death by the hair.

And thus, negligence—which watches for openings and must always be attended to with effort—having found an opening, will strengthen the <s>kleśas</s>. From that, again the recurrence of the undesirable.
Thus, for him not forming attachment and pride, the cultivated object will become firm, and the object to be cultivated will become favorable.
From <s>saṃyama</s> (complete restraint) on the moment (<s>kṣaṇa</s>) and its succession (<s>krama</s>), discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>).

Just as the ultimate limit of substance (<s>dravya</s>) is the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>), so the ultimate limit of time is the moment (<s>kṣaṇa</s>). Or, the time during which a moving atom abandons its former position and attains its next position—that time is a moment.

The uninterrupted flow of those [moments] is succession (<s>krama</s>). There is no real aggregate of moment and succession—it is a mental construct (<s>buddhisamāhāra</s>): <s>muhūrta</s>, day-and-night, and so forth.

This time, though void of real substance, being a mental construction, appearing to follow verbal knowledge—appears to those of ordinary, risen perception as if it were the nature of a real substance.
But the moment is grounded in reality, dependent on succession. And succession, whose nature is the immediacy of moments—the knowers of time call that 'time,' say the <s>yogins</s>.
Two moments cannot exist simultaneously. And succession is impossible between two simultaneous things.
The immediacy of a moment from the prior to the subsequent—that is succession. Therefore, only one present moment exists; past and future moments do not exist.

Therefore there is no aggregate of those. But those past and future moments should be explained as endowed with transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>). By that single moment, the entire world undergoes transformation.
All these <s>dharmas</s> are mounted upon that moment. From <s>saṃyama</s> on those two—the moment and its succession—comes direct perception of them. And from that, discriminative knowledge arises.
Its specific object is being introduced:
From that, discernment of two identical things not differentiated by class (<s>jāti</s>), characteristic (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), and position (<s>deśa</s>).
Of two identical things, when there is similarity of position and characteristic, difference of class is the cause of distinction: 'This is a cow, this is a mare.'
When there is identity of position and class, the characteristic produces distinction: 'This cow is <s>Kālākṣī</s> (black-eyed), this cow is <s>Svastimatī</s> (auspicious).'
Of two <s>āmalaka</s> fruits, when there is similarity of class and characteristic, difference of position produces distinction: 'This is the former, this is the latter.'

But when the former <s>āmalaka</s> is placed in the latter position by a knower occupied with something else, then, due to identity of position, the distinction 'this is the former, this is the latter' cannot be established.
And the knowledge of reality must be free from doubt—therefore it is said: 'From that [discriminative knowledge born of <s>saṃyama</s>], discernment [of identical things].'

How? The position co-momentary with the former <s>āmalaka</s> is different from the position co-momentary with the latter <s>āmalaka</s>. And those <s>āmalakas</s> are differentiated by the experience of their own positional characteristics.
The experience of different positional characteristics is the cause of their distinction.

By this illustration, regarding an atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>) of identical class, characteristic, and position—from the direct perception of the moment co-present with the position of the former atom, the impossibility of that position for the latter atom, and the difference in the co-present moment of the latter's experience of that position—for <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) and the <s>yogin</s>, there arises the cognition of distinction.

Others, however, explain: the ultimate particulars (<s>antyaviśeṣas</s>) produce the cognition of distinction. Even therein, difference of position and characteristic, and difference of form, spatial separation, and class, are the causes of distinction.

But the difference of moments is perceivable only by the intellect of the <s>yogin</s>. Therefore it is said: 'There is no fundamental separateness, because of the absence of difference in form, spatial separation, and class'—so says <s>Vārṣagaṇya</s>.

The discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>) is transcendent (<s>tāraka</s>), has all things as its object (<s>sarvaviṣaya</s>), has all modes as its object (<s>sarvathāviṣaya</s>), and is without succession (<s>akrama</s>).

<s>Tāraka</s> (transcendent): meaning it arises from one's own intuition (<s>pratibhā</s>), not from instruction. <s>Sarvaviṣaya</s> (having all as its object): meaning nothing whatsoever remains beyond its scope.
<s>Sarvathāviṣaya</s> (having all modes as its object): it knows everything—past, present, and future—in all its modes and aspects. This is the meaning.

<s>Akrama</s> (without succession): it grasps everything in all modes mounted upon a single moment. This is the meaning. This discriminative knowledge is complete; its portion is the lamp of <s>yoga</s>, from the honey-like stage onward until its completion.
Whether one has attained or has not attained discriminative knowledge:
When there is equality of purity between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute liberation).

When the <s>buddhi-sattva</s>, having cast off the impurity of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, whose authority extends merely to the discernment of <s>Puruṣa's</s> otherness, with the seeds of <s>kleśas</s> burnt—then it becomes as if resembling <s>Puruṣa</s>. Then the absence of imputed experience for <s>Puruṣa</s> is purity (<s>śuddhi</s>).
In this state, <s>kaivalya</s> occurs—whether for <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) or for the non-lord, whether for one possessing discriminative knowledge or for another.

For one whose seeds of <s>kleśas</s> are burnt, there is no further need of knowledge. This sovereignty and knowledge born of <s>samādhi</s> were initiated through the door of <s>sattva</s>-purity. But in ultimate reality, from knowledge, non-seeing ceases; when that has ceased, there are no further <s>kleśas</s>.

From the absence of <s>kleśas</s>, the absence of <s>karma-vipāka</s> (fruition of action). And the <s>guṇas</s>, their purpose fulfilled in this state, no longer present themselves as objects of perception for <s>Puruṣa</s>.
That is <s>kaivalya</s> of <s>Puruṣa</s>. Then <s>Puruṣa</s>, shining in its own form alone, pure, becomes <s>kevalin</s> (the absolutely liberated one).
<s>Siddhis</s> (supernatural attainments) arise from birth (<s>janma</s>), herbs (<s>oṣadhi</s>), <s>mantras</s>, austerity (<s>tapas</s>), and <s>samādhi</s>.
The <s>siddhi</s> arising from birth is from a different body. [The <s>siddhi</s>] from herbs: through elixirs (<s>rasāyana</s>) in the abodes of <s>Asuras</s>, and so forth.
From <s>mantras</s>: attainment of flying through space, <s>aṇimā</s> (becoming minute), and other [powers].
From austerity (<s>tapas</s>): fulfillment of wishes—taking any desired form, going wherever one wishes, and so forth. The <s>siddhis</s> born of <s>samādhi</s> have [already] been explained.
Therein, when the body and senses have been transformed into another class—
[Sūtra IV.2:] The transformation into another birth (<s>jāti</s>) is due to the overflow (<s>āpūra</s>) of <s>Prakṛti</s>.
The cessation of the prior transformation and the arising of the next transformation [occur] through the entry of new components into them.
And the <s>prakṛtis</s> (natures) of body and senses each support their respective modifications, the overflow awaiting a condition such as <s>dharma</s> and the rest.
[Sūtra IV.3:] The incidental cause does not set the <s>prakṛtis</s> in motion, but rather [causes] the removal of obstacles — from that, like a farmer.

<s>Dharma</s> and the rest, as incidental causes, do not directly activate the <s>prakṛtis</s>; a cause does not propel the effect — how then? Rather, the removal of obstacles from that [cause], like a farmer.

Just as a farmer, wishing to flood another field from a field full of water — whether level, low, or lower still — does not pull the water by hand, but breaks the barrier; when that is broken, the water itself floods the other field; so too <s>dharma</s> breaks the obstructing property of the <s>prakṛtis</s>, and when that is broken, the <s>prakṛtis</s> themselves overflow into their respective modifications.

Or, just as that same farmer, in that very field, is unable to force watery or earthly juices to enter the roots of grain, but rather removes the <s>mudga</s> (mung beans), <s>gaveduka</s>, <s>śyāmāka</s>, and such [weeds] from there.

When those are removed, the juices naturally enter the roots of the grain; similarly, <s>dharma</s> is merely the cause of the cessation of <s>adharma</s>, because of the absolute opposition between purity and impurity — but <s>dharma</s> is not the cause of the activity of <s>prakṛti</s>.

Here <s>Nandīśvara</s> and others are cited as examples. Conversely, <s>adharma</s> also obstructs [<s>dharma</s>]; hence the transformation into impurity. In that regard, <s>Nahuṣa</s>, <s>Ajagara</s>, and others are cited as examples.
But when a <s>yogin</s> creates many bodies, do they have one mind or many minds?
[Sūtra IV.4:] The created minds (<s>nirmāṇacittāni</s>) [arise] from the mere sense of I-am-ness (<s>asmitāmātra</s>) alone.
Taking the mere sense of I-am-ness (<s>asmitāmātra</s>), which is the cause of mind, [the <s>yogin</s>] creates the produced minds; from that they become endowed with minds.
[Sūtra IV.5:] In the differentiation of activities, one mind is the director of the many.
How is it that the activity of many minds is preceded by the intention of one mind? [The <s>yogin</s>] creates one directing mind for all minds; from that arises the differentiation of activities.
[Sūtra IV.6:] Among them, the one born of meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>) is without residual deposit (<s>anāśaya</s>).
The created mind is fivefold: the <s>siddhis</s> (attainments) are those born from birth, herbs, <s>mantras</s>, austerity (<s>tapas</s>), and <s>samādhi</s>.

Among these, only the mind born of meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>) is without residual deposit (<s>āśaya</s>) — it alone has no residual deposit, no activity of desire (<s>rāga</s>) and the rest, hence no connection with merit or demerit, because the <s>yogin</s>'s afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) are destroyed. But the others do have a karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>).
Because:
[Sūtra IV.7:] The <s>karma</s> of a <s>yogin</s> is neither white nor black; for others it is threefold.
This class of <s>karma</s> is indeed fourfold: black, white-and-black, white, and neither-white-nor-black.
Among these, the black belongs to the evil-natured; the white-and-black is accomplished through external means.

In that case, the accumulation of <s>karmāśaya</s> (karmic deposit) occurs only through the door of harming or benefiting others. The white belongs to those engaged in austerity (<s>tapas</s>), self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>), and meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>).
For that [white <s>karma</s>], being dependent on mind alone, is not dependent on external means, and does not arise from harming others.

The neither-white-nor-black belongs to <s>saṃnyāsins</s> (renouncers), those whose afflictions are destroyed, those in their final body. Therein, it is not white because the <s>yogin</s> renounces the fruit, and not black because of non-attachment. But for other beings, it is the former threefold [classification].
[Sūtra IV.8:] From that, the manifestation of only those <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) which correspond to the fruition of that [<s>karma</s>].

'From that' means from the threefold <s>karma</s>; 'corresponding to its fruition' means: whatever class of <s>karma</s>, whatever its fruition, the <s>vāsanās</s> that conform to it — that follow the ripening of <s>karma</s> — of those alone is the manifestation.

For it is not possible that divine <s>karma</s> ripening could be the cause of manifesting <s>vāsanās</s> of hellish, animal, or human [births]. Rather, only <s>vāsanās</s> corresponding to the divine manifest for it. And the same analysis applies to hellish, animal, and human [births].
[Sūtra IV.9:] Even though separated by birth, place, and time, there is continuity [of <s>vāsanās</s>], because of the identity of memory and impressions (<s>saṃskāras</s>).
The ripening of a bull-bite experience manifests through its own revealing conditions.

If that [experience] is separated by a hundred births, or by distant lands, or by a hundred <s>kalpas</s>, and again arises through its own revealing condition — at once, thus the <s>vāsanā</s> conditioned by the previously experienced ripening of a bull-bite would manifest.
Why? Because even for those [<s>vāsanās</s>] that are separated, there is continuity, since a similar <s>karma</s> has become the revealing cause that manifests them.
And why? Because of the identity of memory and impressions. As the experiences, so are the <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions).
And they conform to the <s>karmavāsanās</s> (karmic latent impressions); and as the <s>vāsanās</s>, so the memory — thus from <s>saṃskāras</s> separated by birth, place, and time arises memory.

And from memory arise again <s>saṃskāras</s> — thus these memory-and-impressions manifest by the power of the operation of <s>karmāśaya</s> (karmic deposit). Therefore, even for those separated [by birth, place, and time], since the relation of cause and effect is unbroken, continuity alone is established.
[Sūtra IV.10:] And they (<s>vāsanās</s>) are beginningless, because the desire to live (<s>āśis</s>) is eternal.

Those <s>vāsanās</s> are beginningless because the desire to live is eternal. This self-directed wish — 'May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist' — is seen in every being, and it is not innate [from this life alone].

Why? Because for a creature just born, which has not experienced death, how could there be the fear of death, which has as its cause the memory of the suffering and aversion [associated with death]? And an innate thing does not require a cause.
Therefore, this mind, pervaded by beginningless <s>vāsanās</s>, obtaining certain <s>vāsanās</s> through the force of conditions, revolves for the experience (<s>bhoga</s>) of <s>Puruṣa</s>.

Others hold that the mind, like a pot, palace, or lamp, expands and contracts, and is merely of the size and form of the body. And thus, the intermediate existence (<s>antarābhāva</s>) and <s>saṃsāra</s> are logically consistent.
The teacher [<s>Vyāsa</s>] holds that the mind is all-pervading, and it is its activity (<s>vṛtti</s>) alone that contracts and expands.
And that [activity] depends on conditions such as <s>dharma</s> and the rest. The condition is twofold — external and internal.
The external depends on instruments such as the body and requires praise, gifts, salutations, and the like; the internal, dependent on mind alone, is faith (<s>śraddhā</s>) and the rest.

And thus it has been said: 'Those states of abiding such as friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>) and the rest, practiced by meditators, being independent of external instruments, produce exalted <s>dharma</s>.'
Of the two [kinds of conditions], the mental one is stronger.

How so? Because knowledge and dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) cannot be surpassed by anything; and who could render <s>Daṇḍakāraṇya</s> (the Daṇḍaka forest) empty through bodily action alone, without the power of mind? Or who could drink the ocean like <s>Agastya</s>?
[Sūtra IV.11:] Since they [<s>vāsanās</s>] are held together by cause, effect, substratum, and support — in the absence of these, there is the absence of those.

The cause: from <s>dharma</s> comes pleasure, from <s>adharma</s> comes pain; from pleasure comes desire (<s>rāga</s>), from pain comes aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>); and from those comes effort; through that, exerting oneself by mind, speech, or body, one benefits or harms others; from that again <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion — thus revolves this six-spoked wheel of <s>saṃsāra</s>.
And of this [wheel], revolving moment by moment, <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) is the leader — [as stated:] 'the root of all <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions)' — this is the cause.
The effect is that on the basis of which the present existence of <s>dharma</s> and the rest [occurs], for there is no new arising [without a prior effect].
The mind with its capacity is the substratum (<s>āśraya</s>) of the <s>vāsanās</s>; for when the mind's function has ceased, <s>vāsanās</s> without a substratum cannot persist.
Whatever object is encountered that reveals a particular <s>vāsanā</s> — that [object] is the support (<s>ālambana</s>) of that [<s>vāsanā</s>].
Thus, all <s>vāsanās</s> are held together by these — cause, effect, substratum, and support. In the absence of these, there is also the absence of the <s>vāsanās</s> that depend on them.
'There is no coming into being of what does not exist, nor is there destruction of what exists' — if <s>vāsanās</s> arise as real substances, how will they cease?
[Sūtra IV.12:] Past and future exist in their own nature, due to the difference of time-paths (<s>adhvan</s>) of <s>dharmas</s> (properties).

That which has a future manifestation is the 'not-yet-come' (<s>anāgata</s>); that which has an experienced manifestation is the 'past' (<s>atīta</s>); that which is engaged in its own function is the 'present' (<s>vartamāna</s>). And this threefold reality is the knowable object of knowledge.
And if this did not exist in its own nature, this knowledge would not have arisen without an object.
Therefore, past and future exist in their own nature.

Moreover, if the fruit of <s>karma</s> — whether leading to experience (<s>bhoga</s>) or to liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) — is non-existent when about to arise, then the virtuous practice undertaken for its sake, with that [fruit] as its aim, would not be logically consistent.

And the cause is capable of making the existent fruit present, not of producing something entirely new. It is established that the cause confers a particular determination on the effect — it does not produce it anew.

And the <s>dharmin</s> (substance) has the nature of many <s>dharmas</s> (properties), and its <s>dharmas</s> are established according to the difference of time-phases. But the past and future do not exist in the same way as the present, which is characterized by a specific manifestation, exists as a substance.

The past exists with its own form of having-been-experienced manifestation. The manifestation of own-form belongs only to the present time-phase; that [specific manifestation] does not belong to the past and future time-phases.
And at the time of one time-phase, the other two time-phases exist as connected with the substance (<s>dharmin</s>); thus there is no coming-into-being-from-non-being for the three time-phases.
[Sūtra IV.13:] They are manifest or subtle, having the <s>guṇas</s> as their nature.

These <s>dharmas</s> of the three time-phases — when present, they have a manifest nature; when past or future, they have a subtle nature, being of the form of the six unspecified [<s>aviśeṣa</s>] [categories].

All this is merely a particular arrangement of the <s>guṇas</s> — thus in ultimate reality, they have the <s>guṇas</s> as their nature. And thus the teaching of the <s>śāstra</s>: 'The supreme form of the <s>guṇas</s> does not come within the range of sight; but that which comes within the range of sight is as trivial as an illusion (<s>māyā</s>).'
But if everything consists of <s>guṇas</s>, how can there be one sound, one sense organ?
[Sūtra IV.14:] The reality of a thing is due to the unity of transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>).

One transformation of the <s>guṇas</s> — whose character is illumination (<s>prakhyā</s>), activity (<s>kriyā</s>), and stability (<s>sthiti</s>), and which are of the nature of apprehension — into the state of an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>) is the sense organ of hearing; one transformation of those [<s>guṇas</s>] which are of the nature of the apprehensible into the state of the sound <s>tanmātra</s> (subtle element) is 'sound,' the object. Of sounds and the rest, which belong to the same class as material forms, one transformation is the earth atom (<s>pṛthivī-paramāṇu</s>), a component of the <s>tanmātras</s>; and one transformation of those is earth, cow, tree, mountain, and so forth. In other elements too, incorporating heat, warmth, fluidity, and space-giving, the general principle of a single unified product should be understood.

There is no object coexistent with consciousness, but there is knowledge coexistent with objects, imagined as in dreams and the like — in this direction, those who deny the true nature of things, [saying] 'reality is merely the construction of knowledge, comparable to dream-objects, not existing in the ultimate sense' — how could they, abandoning the real nature of things that presents itself by its own power, denying that very [reality] through the force of conceptual knowledge that lacks valid means of proof, have their words be credible?
And why is this unreasonable?
[Sūtra:] When the object is the same, due to the difference of minds, the two [object and mind] have separate paths.
A single object, common [to all], which has become the support of many minds — that is indeed neither imagined by one mind nor by many minds, but is self-established.

How [is this so]? Due to the difference of minds regarding the same object. Depending on merit, even though the object is the same, pleasant knowledge arises for the mind; depending on demerit, painful knowledge from that same [object]; depending on ignorance, deluded knowledge from that same [object]; depending on right vision, knowledge of equanimity from that same [object].
By whose mind was that [object] imagined? And it is not reasonable that an object imagined by one mind should color another's mind.
Therefore, the paths of object and knowledge, which differ as graspable and grasping, are separate. There is not even a trace of intermixture between them.

According to the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position, moreover, the object — being threefold [in its <s>guṇas</s>], mutable, and functioning through the <s>guṇas</s> — is connected with minds depending on the operative cause of merit and the like.
And it becomes the cause, in its respective form, of the cognition that arises in accordance with the operative cause.
Some say:

'The object is coexistent with knowledge alone, because it is to be experienced, like pleasure and the like.' Through this approach, while obstructing the commonality [of the object], they deny the very form of the object in the preceding and succeeding moments.
[Sūtra:] If the object were dependent on a single mind, when not cognized by that [mind], what would it be?

If the object were dependent on a single mind, then when the mind is distracted or restrained — its very nature not grasped by that [mind], not having become an object for another, without valid cognition, with its nature unapprehended by anyone — what would it then be?

And when it is again connected with a mind, whence would it arise? And those parts of it that were not present [to the mind] would not exist for it — thus, if 'the back does not exist,' then even the belly would not be apprehended.

Therefore, the object is independent and common to all <s>puruṣas</s>; and the minds function independently for each <s>puruṣa</s>. From the connection of the two [object and mind], apprehension [arises]; for <s>Puruṣa</s>, [this constitutes] experience.
[Sūtra:] An object is known or unknown to the mind depending on whether it colors [the mind].
The sense-objects, like lodestones, having connected with the mind which is like iron, color it.
The sense-object by which the mind is colored — that object is known; another, however, is unknown. Because objects have the nature of being known or unknown, the mind is subject to transformation.
But for him whose object is that very mind:
[Sūtra:] The modifications of the mind are always known to its lord, <s>Puruṣa</s>, due to his unchanging nature.

If <s>Puruṣa</s>, the lord, were also to undergo transformation like the mind, then the mental modifications which are his objects would be sometimes known and sometimes unknown, like objects of sound and the like. But the fact that the mind is always known leads to the inference that its lord, <s>Puruṣa</s>, is unchanging.
An objection might be raised: 'The mind itself will be self-luminous and object-luminous, like fire' —
[Sūtra:] It [the mind] is not self-luminous, because it is an object of perception.
Just as the other sense-organs and sound and the like are not self-luminous because they are objects of perception, so too should the mind be understood.

And fire is not an apt illustration here. For fire does not illuminate its own nature that was previously unilluminated. Moreover, this illumination is observed [only] in the conjunction of the illuminable and the illuminator.
And there is no conjunction in [something's] own nature alone. Moreover, 'the mind is self-luminous' would mean it is ungraspable by anyone — this is the implication of the statement.

Just as space is self-established and not dependent on another — this is the meaning. From the self-awareness of the workings of one's own intellect, the activity of beings is observed: 'I am angry,' 'I am afraid,' 'here is my attachment,' 'there is my anger.' This would not be possible without the apprehension of one's own intellect.
[Sūtra:] And [if the mind were self-luminous], both [self and object] could not be determined simultaneously.

And it is not reasonable that one's own nature and another's nature be determined in a single moment; for those who hold the doctrine of momentariness accept that existence itself is action and is also the agent.
One might think: 'The mind, [naturally] restrained by its own momentum, is grasped by another immediately succeeding mind.'
[Sūtra:] If [the mind were] perceived by another mind, there would be an infinite regress of cognition of cognition, and confusion of memories.
If the mind were grasped by another mind, by what would the cognition of that cognition be grasped? 'That too by another, that too by another' — thus there is an infinite regress.
And there would be confusion of memories, for as many as are the experiences of cognitions-of-cognitions, that many memories would result.

And from the confusion of these, there would be the inability to determine even a single memory. Thus, by the <s>Vaināśikas</s> (destructionists / Buddhists) who deny <s>Puruṣa</s> as the one who is aware of cognition, everything has been thrown into utter confusion.

They, however, postulating the nature of the experiencer in various ways, cannot arrive at a logically consistent position. Some, having postulated even a mere 'being' (<s>sattva</s>) — 'there is that being which, having cast off these five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), takes up others' — after having said this, then recoil from that very [position].

Likewise, having said 'I shall live the holy life (<s>brahmacarya</s>) in the presence of the teacher, for the sake of great disenchantment with the <s>skandhas</s>, for dispassion, for non-arising, for peace' — they then deny the very being (<s>sattva</s>) [that undertakes this].
The doctrines of <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, <s>Yoga</s>, and the like, however, with their own terminology, arrive at <s>Puruṣa</s> alone as the owner and experiencer of the mind.
How?
[Sūtra:] When [the mind] assumes the form of that [unchanging consciousness], there is self-awareness of one's own intellect — by virtue of <s>citi</s> (pure awareness) which does not transfer.
For the experiencer-power, being unchanging and non-transferring, yet as if transferred to the transforming object, follows the modifications [of the mind].

And the cognitive function — being merely an imitation of the intellectual modification that has acquired the character of being grasped by consciousness — is described as indistinguishable from the intellectual modification.
And thus it has been said:

'Not in the netherworld, nor in the caverns of mountains, nor in the darkness, nor in the bellies of the oceans — the cave in which the eternal <s>Brahman</s> is deposited, the sages know [to be] the intellectual modification which is [seemingly] indistinguishable [from it].'
And from this, this [conclusion] is accepted:
[Sūtra:] The mind, colored by the seer and the seen, [comprehends] all objects.

For the mind, colored by the object to be cognized, being itself an object, is connected through its own modification with <s>Puruṣa</s>, the subject. Thus this very mind, colored by both seer and seen, reflecting both object and subject, having assumed the nature of both conscious and unconscious — though of the nature of an object, appearing as if not an object; though unconscious, appearing as if conscious; like a crystal-gem — is said to [comprehend] all objects.

Thus, some, deluded by this resemblance of the mind [to consciousness], say that it alone is conscious. Others [say]: 'All this is nothing but mind alone; this world with its cows and pots and the like, together with its causes, does not truly exist.'
They are not to be entertained. Why? Because they have a seed of delusion — [namely the assumption that] the mind reflects the forms and appearances of all things.
In the wisdom born of <s>samādhi</s>, the object to be known is [present as] a reflection, and being the support [of cognition], it is other [than the cognition itself].

If that object were nothing but mind, how could the form of wisdom be determined by wisdom itself? Therefore, the object present as a reflection in wisdom, and that by which it is determined — that is <s>Puruṣa</s>.
Thus, from the distinction of the mind into the natures of grasper, grasping, and graspable, those who see correctly differentiate all three by their kind; by them, <s>Puruṣa</s> is realized.
And for what reason [does the mind exist for another]?
[Sūtra:] Though variegated by innumerable <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions), it [the mind] exists for another's purpose, because it acts in combination.

This very mind, though variegated by innumerable <s>vāsanās</s>, exists for another's purpose — for the sake of another's experience and liberation — not for its own purpose, because it acts in combination, like a house.

The mind, which acts in combination, cannot exist for its own purpose; a pleasure-cognition is not for the sake of pleasure, nor is knowledge for the sake of knowledge — both of these exist for another's purpose.
And that <s>Puruṣa</s> for whose purpose there is experience and liberation, and who is not [himself] of the nature of an object — he alone is the other, [though] a mere universal.

Whatever the <s>Vaināśika</s> (destructionist) might cite as that other — a mere universal, a self-nature — all of that, because it acts in combination, would exist for another's purpose. But that other, the particular — he, <s>Puruṣa</s>, is not one who acts in combination.
[Sūtra:] For one who sees the distinction, there is the cessation of speculation about the nature of the self.

Just as the sprouting of grass-blades in the rainy season leads to the inference of the existence of their seeds, so too, when upon hearing the path to liberation one's hair stands on end and tears flow, it is inferred that there too exists the seed of the vision of distinction — a <s>karma</s> conducive to liberation that has come to fruition.

For such a one, the natural speculation about the nature of the self proceeds; and in the absence of this [seed], it is said that, leaving aside their natural disposition, some develop an inclination toward the objection but a disinclination toward the conclusion. Therein, the speculation about the nature of the self is: 'Who was I? How was I? What indeed is this? How indeed is this? What shall we become? How shall we become?'

But for one who sees the distinction, that [speculation] ceases. Why? Because this manifold transformation belongs to the mind alone; <s>Puruṣa</s>, when <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) does not exist, is pure and untouched by the properties of the mind.
Therefore, for one who is skilled [in discrimination], the speculation about the nature of the self ceases.
[Sūtra:] Then the mind inclines toward discrimination and gravitates toward <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation).

At that time, that mind of his which was gravitating toward objects and inclining toward ignorance becomes otherwise — gravitating toward <s>kaivalya</s> and inclining toward the knowledge born of discrimination.
[Sūtra:] In the intervals of that [discriminative awareness], other cognitions [arise] from <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions).

For the mind whose flow is inclined toward discriminative discernment (<s>pratyayaviveka</s>), carrying only the knowledge of the distinction between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, in its gaps there arise other cognitions: 'I am,' or 'this is mine,' or 'I know,' or 'I do not know.'
Whence [do they arise]? From the previous <s>saṃskāras</s> (latent impressions) whose seeds are diminishing.
Their destruction has been described as being like that of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions).

Just as the <s>kleśas</s>, when their seeds are burnt, are no longer capable of sprouting, so too the previous <s>saṃskāras</s>, their seeds being burnt by the fire of knowledge, no longer produce cognitions.
But the <s>saṃskāras</s> of knowledge rest until the completion of the mind's function—thus they are understood.

For one who is without self-interest even in the highest meditation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), there is, through constant discriminative discernment (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>), the <s>dharmamegha</s> (cloud of dharma) <s>samādhi</s>. [YS 4.29]
When this <s>brāhmaṇa</s> is without self-interest even in the highest meditation—desiring nothing whatsoever even from that—

for one who is dispassionate even toward that, there arises only constant discriminative discernment; and through the exhaustion of the seeds of <s>saṃskāras</s>, no other cognitions arise for him. Then his <s>samādhi</s> is called <s>dharmamegha</s> (cloud of dharma).
From that, the cessation of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and <s>karma</s>. [YS 4.30]

From the attainment of that [<s>dharmamegha samādhi</s>], the <s>kleśas</s> beginning with <s>avidyā</s> are uprooted, pulled out with their roots. And the repositories of <s>karma</s>, both wholesome and unwholesome, are destroyed, annihilated at their root.

With the cessation of <s>kleśas</s> and <s>karma</s>, the wise one becomes liberated while still living. Why? Because error (<s>viparyaya</s>) is the cause of [continued] existence. For no one whose error has been destroyed is ever seen born anywhere, by any means.
Then, for knowledge freed from all its veils and impurities, due to its infinitude, what remains to be known is little. [YS 4.31]
For knowledge liberated from all veils of <s>kleśas</s> and <s>karma</s>, there is infinitude.
The infinite <s>sattva</s> of knowledge, overpowered and veiled by the obscuring <s>tamas</s>, is set in motion by <s>rajas</s> here and there, [and when] uncovered, becomes capable of apprehension.
Therein, when it is freed from all veiling impurities, then its infinitude arises.
Due to the infinitude of knowledge, what remains to be known becomes small—like a firefly in space.
Where this has been stated:
'A blind man pierced the jewel; a fingerless one threaded it; a neckless one put it on; a tongueless one praised it.'
Then, for the <s>guṇas</s> whose purpose is fulfilled, there is the completion of the sequence of transformations. [YS 4.32]

From the arising of that <s>dharmamegha</s> [<s>samādhi</s>], the sequence of transformations of the <s>guṇas</s> whose purpose is fulfilled comes to completion. For [the <s>guṇas</s>] whose experience and liberation have been accomplished, whose sequence is completed, cannot endure even for a moment.
Now, what is this 'sequence' (<s>krama</s>)?
Sequence (<s>krama</s>) is the counterpart of a moment, apprehensible at the final point of a transformation. [YS 4.33]

Sequence, whose nature is the succession of moments, is apprehended at the final point—the conclusion—of a transformation. For oldness of a cloth at its end does not occur without moments of sequence having been experienced. And sequence is observed in permanent things.
And this permanence is of two kinds: the permanence of the immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>) and the permanence of the ever-transforming (<s>pariṇāmin</s>).
Therein, immutable permanence belongs to <s>Puruṣa</s>; transforming permanence belongs to the <s>guṇas</s>.
That in which the essential nature is not destroyed while undergoing transformation—that is permanent. And since the essential nature of both is not destroyed, both are permanent.

Therein, in the properties of the <s>guṇas</s>, such as <s>buddhi</s> and the rest, the sequence apprehensible at the final point of transformation reaches its conclusion; but in the permanent substance, the <s>guṇas</s>, it does not reach a conclusion.

In the immutably permanent liberated <s>Puruṣas</s>, established in their own nature alone, existence in one's own form is experienced only through sequence—and there too, it does not reach a conclusion, being conceptually constructed on the basis of the word 'is,' taking the verb of existence.
Now, does this <s>saṃsāra</s>, which operates through the <s>guṇas</s>, have a completion of sequence—its continuance and movement—or not?
This is unanswerable. How so? There are questions that are categorically answerable: 'Everyone born will die.' 'Indeed so.'
Now, [the question:] 'Will everyone who has died be reborn?' This is to be answered with a distinction.
One in whom discriminative knowledge has arisen, whose craving is exhausted—the wise one—will not be reborn; the other, however, will be reborn.
Similarly, [the question:] 'Is human birth superior or not?' When asked thus, the answer requires a distinction: it is superior with respect to animals; not superior with respect to gods and sages.
But this question is unanswerable: 'Is this <s>saṃsāra</s> finite or infinite?'
For the wise one, there is a completion of the sequence of <s>saṃsāra</s>; not for the other—in the determination of either alternative lies a fault. Therefore this question is indeed unanswerable.
Having stated <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute liberation) as the completion of the sequence of the function of the <s>guṇas</s>, its essential nature is now determined:

<s>Kaivalya</s> (liberation) is the involution (<s>pratiprasava</s>) of the <s>guṇas</s>, devoid of the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>; or it is the power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>) established in its own nature. [YS 4.34]

The involution of the <s>guṇas</s>—which are of the nature of cause and effect—whose purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> (experience and liberation) is fulfilled, devoid of [further] purpose—that is <s>kaivalya</s>. And establishment in one's own nature means: since <s>Puruṣa</s> is no longer connected with the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>, the power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>) alone remains in isolation; its abiding forever thus is <s>kaivalya</s>.
